# MDX-3.0 Loading Requirements Evolution

## 2023-04-19 Opening Paragraph

This page was originally created because two terms in MDX-3.0 were placed on the same investigation path: `export-map JSX resolution` and `Node loader hook ordering`. The file we could trace directly to at the time was `packages/loader/lib/index.js`. The adjacency visible in the file header was limited:

```js
import {Buffer} from 'node:buffer'
import {createHash} from 'node:crypto'
import path from 'node:path'
import {createFormatAwareProcessors} from '@mdx-js/mdx/lib/util/create-format-aware-processors.js'
```

These lines gave the subsequent investigation a shared starting point. `path` is a visible path-handling clue, and `createFormatAwareProcessors` indicates that the loader file is adjacent to the processor construction; `Buffer` and `createHash` also appear in the file header. They only mean that these objects warrant attention during review. The import order cannot directly establish the source of the JSX runtime, nor the order in which the hooks execute.

The early record placed two questions too close together: whether the JSX runtime name in the export map could still be resolved, and whether a subsequent hook would take over after the loader had processed it once. At the time, they were not treated as two separate questions. This left an unverified working assumption: when no public-name match was found, processing might continue if a filesystem path could be constructed.

The assumption seemed fairly permissive at the time. Looking up the public name through the export map means first accepting the package-declared export; converting it to a path seemed to leave room for legacy callers. But the record contains neither a match result nor a no-match result, much less any indication whether the constructed path belongs to a public entry point of the package. It can therefore only serve as an investigation direction, not be written as a compatibility promise.

## Options Kept Open

No complete approach was selected at that time; two paths were left for comparison:

- Continue checking the public name through the export map, and record where the loader interprets the name;
- When the name cannot be found, try path handling and observe whether the loader can continue.

The first path concerns the name exposed by the package. The second concerns whether a local path can be constructed. They are not the same thing merely because both occur near the loader. In particular, the existence of a path does not by itself mean that the path should be treated as a public export.

This version still has no standalone evidence for `Node loader hook ordering`. There is no short example, no record of return points, and no result showing a hook's relative order. The fact that a single runtime can load is not enough to prove that other hook combinations will work in the same order.

## Leave It at the File Boundary for Now

This version retains only `packages/loader/lib/index.js` as an entry point for revisiting the issue, without expanding it into the entire processing chain. Subsequent review should verify name resolution and hook returns separately: start with the export map for the former; the latter requires directly observing where the loader processes it. This page originally started with `packages/loader/lib/index.js`. The direct dependencies at the top of the file are as follows:

```js
import {Buffer} from 'node:buffer'
import {createHash} from 'node:crypto'
import path from 'node:path'
import {createFormatAwareProcessors} from '@mdx-js/mdx/lib/util/create-format-aware-processors.js'
```

The initial version treated this file only as a loader file that could be traced further. The actual question at the time was not "whether the file exists", but whether the JSX runtime name in the export map still followed the package's public entry point after passing through the loader. The opening paragraph placed two issues too close together: whether resolution could fall back to a filesystem path if the public name did not match; whether later processing would still pick it up if a hook had already handled it once. After review, these two questions need to be separated.

`path` at the top of the file once made path fallback seem convenient. `createFormatAwareProcessors` made it easy to discuss processor construction and name resolution together. In retrospect, these were only adjacent clues. The fact that `Buffer`, `createHash`, `path`, and the processor import appear at the top of the same file does not prove that they jointly determine the export for the JSX runtime, let alone provide evidence of Node hook ordering.

### The Old Assessment, Kept for Now

> When the public JSX runtime cannot be found, first try converting the name to a file path; if the path exists, processing can continue.

This was a working assessment left over from the initial version, not a subsequently confirmed conclusion. It has no corresponding match and no-match results, nor does it state whether that path is one of the package's public exports. It is retained because the early investigation really did start in this direction; deleting it outright would leave the later corrections without their context.

At the time, "a path can be constructed" and "a name can be resolved publicly" were treated as similar indicators of success. The review needs to separate them. Being able to construct a path only means that there is a representable local filesystem path; public resolution requires first checking whether the export map provides that name. The former cannot replace the latter.

## 2024 Review Addendum

This review did not turn the file into an end-to-end explanation, but only split the original question into two narrower parts.

The first part is `export-map JSX resolution`. Checks should start with the name itself: whether the name is still the one requested by the caller, whether the export map provides a public export, and whether the loader changes how the name is interpreted in the process. If the name does not match, it must not first be rewritten as a path and then have that path's reachability used as proof that the original name is usable.

The second part is `Node loader hook ordering`. What is needed here is the order of hooks and where control goes after they return, not the result of one successful load. Being able to load a runtime may only mean that the request did not fail immediately at some point; it does not show whether another hook has already seen the request, nor whether another stage of processing follows the return.

Both parts are closely related to the loader, but each requires different observations. Name resolution requires a record of the public mappings in the export map. The ordering question requires a record of whether processing stops or continues after a hook returns. If they are combined into a single statement that "the loader can handle the runtime", the earlier confusion will reappear.

### Flaws in the Old Investigation Order

The old notes once listed the steps as follows:

```text
First check whether a filename can be constructed from the path
Then check whether the JSX runtime can be loaded
Finally revisit the export map
```

This sequence is no longer suitable as an order for making judgments. It first treats the path as a known entity, then determines whether the package exposes the name; once a path can be constructed, readers can easily treat the filesystem path as an acceptable export. The old sequence is retained to explain why the initial version leaned toward path fallback.

The alternative approach has not been written up as a new operating manual, and only three points of observation remain: what the original name is, whether the export map provides a public export, and whether the next hook is entered after the loader returns. The third point cannot be inferred from the first two, nor should it be assumed to have been confirmed just because the first two succeed.

## Boundary with the Adjacent Interface Issue

DOC-12 is recorded as an adjacent entry point. It discusses short-circuit module return and structured runtime causes. This page overlaps with it at module return: this page needs to know whether processing continues after the loader returns, while DOC-12 addresses how interface return values express structured causes.

These two subjects should not stand in for each other. Seeing short-circuit module return does not directly establish Node loader hook ordering; seeing structured runtime causes does not fill in this page's export map resolution results either. The existence of DOC-12 only provides an interface-related direction for further investigation during review.

## What Could Be Decided at the Time

After review, public names can be the first thing checked for name resolution. A filesystem path can be retained as an old investigative hypothesis, but must not be treated as a default fallback. This decision does not claim that all existing callers can continue to work through non-public paths; the initial version left no such results, and the review did not add any.

On hook ordering, the only decision that can be made is not to present unconfirmed observations as stable behavior. If the investigation reaches `packages/loader/lib/index.js`, the name, the export map result, and whether the next hook is entered should be recorded separately. There are no new commands, caller examples, or reproducible outputs here, so no seemingly precise execution chain is being added.

## What Remains Blank

This review confirmed the need to split the question, but did not produce a real example short enough to illustrate Node loader hook ordering. The gaps do not mean hooks are irrelevant, but that the ordering cannot be inferred from the top of the file, path handling, or a single runtime load.

If the investigation continues, it must at least distinguish two kinds of result: the name itself has no public export, or the name has been handled but the behavior of subsequent hooks is unknown. The former concerns the relationship between the export map and the JSX runtime, while the latter concerns execution order. Calling both cases "loader failure" would mix the old assessments together again.

Tentative decision: continue checking name resolution against public entry points; retain filesystem path only as an old hypothesis; Node loader hook ordering awaits direct, localized observations.

# MDX-3.0 History of Loading Requirements

## 2023-04-19, starting with a single file

When this page was first written, there was only one very specific starting point for tracing back:`packages/loader/lib/index.js`. The issue was labeled `export-map JSX resolution / Node loader hook ordering`, but the file itself did not distinguish these two issues for us. Four direct dependencies were visible in the file header:

```js
import {Buffer} from 'node:buffer'
import {createHash} from 'node:crypto'
import path from 'node:path'
import {createFormatAwareProcessors} from '@mdx-js/mdx/lib/util/create-format-aware-processors.js'
```

The approach at the time was straightforward: first record the file, then look back using the terms `export`,`map`,`loader` and `path` as leads. That page had no complete call graph, nor did it describe the file as the main entry point for the entire MDX processing chain. We could confirm that, as part of an existing js module, the file was suitable for code reading and checking historical behavior; the file header provided only local adjacency, so not all implementation decisions could be attributed to this file.

The opening paragraph recorded an unverified working hypothesis: if the public JSX runtime name did not match directly, converting it to a filesystem path might be more likely to keep legacy callers working than continuing down the export map branch. This hypothesis was not accompanied by any match output, nor did it state whether that path was one the package publicly exposed. The original wording is retained here for now, because it does reflect the direction of the investigation at the time.

That record did not settle on a complete solution. The two paths left open were:

- Continue investigating the public names in the export map, and record where the names are interpreted;
- Try path handling when a name cannot be found, and observe whether the downstream loader still works.

The difference between the two paths was described at the time as "stricter" versus "more compatible", but those two terms were too vague, so they could not later be used directly as grounds for a decision. In particular, there was no record of whether the second path would bypass the exports the package had already declared.

## Limitations Alongside the File Header

`node:path` made path handling a visible lead, and `createFormatAwareProcessors` made processor another lead.`Buffer` and `createHash` were also in the same import block, but the early page did not force a connection between them and JSX runtime resolution. That incompleteness is preserved here: the file header can tell later readers where to look first, but it cannot fill in nonexistent call relationships for them.

This boundary was not made clear in the first version. Seeing `path` does not mean it has been confirmed that a name will be rewritten as a path; seeing the processor's construction dependencies does not mean that the processor determines the entry points exposed by the export map. Looking back later, it was precisely these adjacent objects that made it easy to mistake "being able to keep reading the code" for "already knowing the behavior".

At this stage, Node loader hook ordering was only a related issue mentioned in the title. There was no stable, short example, no ordering table, and not enough evidence to generalize a single loading result to different hook combinations. The early conclusion therefore went no further than "needs to be checked again".

## After the spring of 2023, the issue was split into two tracks

Later addenda separated what had originally been a tangle of issues. The first track was name resolution: whether the names exposed in the export map were preserved, and whether the loader interpreted them as another entry point. The second was execution order: after a given hook returned, whether subsequent processing continued or the current module return was already complete.

This separation changed how the decision record was written. A name resolution result cannot prove that hooks have been ordered as expected; an observation about hook order likewise cannot, in turn, prove that a particular filesystem path is a public entry point. Both can appear near the same file, but they provide evidence about different things.

The old passage from 2023 is still retained here:

> If there is no match for the public name, first convert it to a file path; as long as the path exists, processing can continue.

This passage was later marked **deprecated**. It describes the working assumption at the time, not the current rule. The reason for deprecating it was not as simple as "the path is necessarily invalid", but rather that "the path exists" and "the path is publicly exported" are not the same thing. The early page did not distinguish between these two conditions, so it cannot be edited to read as current guidance.

## Review addendum for 2024-01-17

During the review, there was only one actionable change: check the export map first, then how the loader handles names; do not infer a fallback strategy from a `path` import at the top of a file. This order was intended to prevent the old record from describing "can be located" as "can be used".

The review also required leaving hook ordering as a separate blank item. A blank item did not mean that hooks were unimportant, but that at the time there was no real example short enough to include on this page. If a future addition merely said "the order is now fixed", readers would still not know which hook, at which return point, or on which runtime it was observed, so this version did not say that.

During the same period, DOC-12 was recorded as an adjacent entry. Its topic is short-circuit module return / structured runtime causes. The two pages meet at module return: DOC-12 focuses on how interface return values carry structured causes, while this page focuses on name resolution and hook ordering on the loader side. The topic of DOC-12 must not be used to supply this page with a conclusion about Node behavior that it does not contain.

During review, "successful loading" was also downgraded from a conclusion to an observation. Successful loading only shows that a particular entry attempt did not immediately abort; it does not show that another export-map name will produce the same result, nor does it show that all Node hooks execute in the same order. This distinction did not produce a new, complete workflow, but it meant that the old path assumptions could no longer serve as default rules.

## An old processing sequence that was not removed

The old notes once laid out the troubleshooting steps as follows:

```text
First check whether the path can form a filename
Then check whether loading works in the JSX runtime
Finally revisit the export map
```

This sequence was later marked **later overturned**. The problem was that it first treated the path as a known object and only then evaluated the export map; once a path could be constructed, it was easy to treat a filesystem path as a valid package export. This passage is still visible when looking back now, but it only shows how the old troubleshooting process began, not how results should be interpreted today.

The replacement sequence was not expanded into a new tutorial, leaving only three observation points: what the name is exactly as given, whether the export map provides a public export, and whether there are subsequent hooks after the loader returns. The third observation point concerns Node loader hook ordering and cannot be derived by combining the first two observation points.

These three observation points also have different stopping points. While the name is still a name, you can continue by checking the export map; when the export map does not provide a public export, that result should not be skipped in order to prove that some local path is reachable; whether subsequent processing occurs at the return point must be left to direct observation on the hook side. Stopping a check at the first two points does not prevent leaving the third unknown.

## Test record: one success is not enough for closure

The recheck record from 2024 did not preserve commands or caller code, only the result at the level of "one actual recheck was added, and the parts not yet confirmed were retained". Therefore, no seemingly precise execution output is fabricated here.

At the time, the available material still consisted of file paths, direct dependencies in file headers, and local code navigation. The review separated successful loading from confirmation of ordering: successful loading only shows that this entry point did not fail immediately on this occasion; it does not show that another export-map name would produce the same result, nor does it show that all Node hooks execute in the same order.

This step had a practical impact on the decision. The old filesystem path assumption could no longer be included in the current guidance as the default strategy; but because there was no complete failure case, the page did not expand the opposite position into a compatibility matrix either. The decision covered only the export relationships that could already be confirmed, leaving unconfirmed ordering for a later section.

The gaps in the test material also explain why two complete paths, "normal" and "abnormal," were not provided. The existing records are only sufficient to require that both hits and misses be retained in the future, not to supply specific results for either case. Filling the blanks with typical output would only replace the missing firsthand evidence with new speculation.

## New clues on the card from 2025

By 2025-09, the public material from MDX-201 still stated `export-map JSX resolution still has one unconfirmed point.` This record did not provide a complete case that could be transcribed onto this page, so it only changed the status: the issue had not been fully closed by a single early review. MDX-201 also retained the public contract wording `export-map-only JSX runtime`; that term is suitable as a starting point for searches, but cannot be treated as an implementation description.

Another record from MDX-201 required retaining one hit result and one miss result. This requirement sits right alongside the lack of output on the early page, but this page has not fabricated those two results. It shows that the next check needs to present a positive case and a negative case side by side, rather than posting only one successful path. Nor did this requirement cause this page to change its historical assessment of the old version: the old version did not have these materials at the time.

MDX-216 recorded a counterexample action in 2025-10. A correction then appeared in the card:

> A correction: in the loader and runtime dispatch section, there is still one unconfirmed point regarding Node loader hook ordering.

This correction supersedes the tendency in the old paragraph that "order can roughly be inferred from a single dispatch." It does not provide the final ordering, nor does it authorize this page to present unconfirmed parts as stable interfaces. Here, "correction" only corrects the scope of understanding: observing runtime dispatch cannot replace direct examples of hook ordering.

The unconfirmed items from the two cards cannot be merged into one vague loader issue. MDX-201 leave a gap in name resolution; MDX-216 leave an ordering gap in dispatch adjacency. They can be seen in the same follow-up review, but they stop at different observation points.

## The two choices on the review table

Once the materials from each round are put together, the choices in the decision record can be read as follows:

**Choice one: treat path fallback as a resolution rule.**

The advantage is that it is easy to continue the old investigation, and the file header already contains `path` as a visible clue. The cost is that "path exists" obscures the boundary of the export map and makes a non-public filesystem path look like a legitimate JSX runtime entry point. Earlier records leaned toward this choice, but no hit output or failure output supports it.

It also has a subtle problem: path fallback ties name resolution to execution order. After some path handling, runtime may continue to work, causing readers to mistakenly infer that the name itself has already been legally resolved, or that the position of a subsequent hook has already been determined. In fact, these three judgments do not amount to the same result.

**Choice two: first handle the name according to the export map's public names.**

The advantage is that the question is clear: first ask whether the package publicly exposes this name, then see how the loader proceeds. The cost is that if legacy callers depend on a non-public path, that dependency cannot be preserved automatically merely because the path can be constructed. This choice requires recording the absence of a public export separately from hook ordering; otherwise, when it fails, we will still fall back to the first old interpretation.

Choice two does not require this page to declare that all export-map branches have already been exhausted. It only establishes the order of judgment for name resolution: public exposure comes before path reachability. If public exposure has not been confirmed, another filesystem path cannot be used to make it "compatible"; if public exposure has been confirmed, hook ordering may still remain unknown.

The decision made on this page is to adopt the second direction as the current name-resolution policy. This decision covers only the public export relationship between export-map and JSX runtime; it does not also declare Node loader hook ordering complete. The latter still requires a local example that can be processed again.

## State diagram left during the follow-up review

The diagram below marks only the decision points already distinguished on this page. It is not a hook ordering diagram, nor does it disguise an unconfirmed state as a completed transition.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NameCheck
    NameCheck --> PublicExportCheck: Preserve the original name
    NameCheck --> NoNameMatch: No name result obtained
    PublicExportCheck --> loaderReturnPoint: export map provides a public export
    PublicExportCheck --> NoNameMatch: No public export observed
    loaderReturnPoint --> hookOrderPendingConfirmation: Subsequent processing requires separate observation
    NoNameMatch --> [*]
    hookOrderPendingConfirmation --> [*]
```

"NoNameMatch" in the diagram does not mean that the file does not exist, nor does it mean that a path should be constructed immediately. "hookOrderPendingConfirmation" also does not mean that the loader did not work. The two endpoints preserve distinct gaps in name resolution and execution order, respectively.

## Current formulation, placed here rather than at the beginning

After the earlier old passages, review addendum, overturned processing order, card counterexamples, and corrections, the behavior that currently needs to be preserved is:

> The loader resolves an export-map-only JSX runtime without falling back to an unexported filesystem path.

This sentence is the precise formulation for the current version. It corrects the opening paragraph's assumption that "processing can continue as long as the path exists", and clarifies the boundary between the export map's decision and filesystem path fallback. It does not describe the full Node loader hook ordering; the two cannot be combined into a broader conclusion.

Therefore, the current starting point for verifying `packages/loader/lib/index.js` remains limited in scope: first use the name to check the public export relationship in the export map, then follow the loader's return point to see whether subsequent processing occurs. If the subject of observation is runtime dispatch, the position of hook ordering must also be marked separately; the dispatch result cannot be treated directly as proof of ordering.

This formulation also does not make `path` in the file header irrelevant. Path handling may still be encountered when reading individual sections of the code, but it no longer serves as "the automatic exit after a public name lookup has no match". Keeping the old import is meant to help locate the old check, not bring that check back into the decision.

## Which section is responsible for which objects

| Object | What this page can establish | What this page does not supply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `packages/loader/lib/index.js` | An entry point for loader-side code reading and historical cross-checking | A call graph for the entire repository |
| The JSX runtime name in the export map | Check whether the public export exists | Package configuration details that were not provided |
| unexported filesystem path | A boundary counterexample to the old assumption | Turning it back into a compatibility entry point |
| Node loader hook ordering | Record ordering questions that remain to be confirmed | A complete ordering unsupported by the available material |
| `createFormatAwareProcessors` | A direct adjacency clue in the file header | Inferring which dispatch the processor participated in |
| DOC-12 | Navigation for reviews of adjacent interfaces | Using it as a substitute for this page's loader decision |

This table defines boundaries added later, not what the early page originally looked like. The early page placed "the file is here" and "the implementation decision is here" very close together; now only the former's navigational role is retained.`Buffer`,`createHash`,`path` and processor import can still help readers locate specific parts, but they do not automatically constitute evidence of behavior.

The table lists DOC-12 separately to prevent another common source of confusion. The short-circuit module return may be adjacent to this page's return point, and structured runtime causes may also show the same runtime context to the person investigating; but which causes an interface return carries, and whether the loader resolves the JSX runtime based on public exports, remain two separate lines of inquiry.

## Sequence recorded during the review

For name resolution issues, record the original name first, rather than rewriting it as a path first. Then examine the public relationships provided by the export map. If the result involves the JSX runtime, also record the loader's return point separately. Only by doing this, can you avoid interpreting a miss directly as "the file does not exist", or interpreting it as "we can proceed" just because a path can be constructed locally.

For hook issues, it is sufficient to record the following three adjacent points:

- Which loader hook sees the request first;
- Which return indicates whether the current module has short-circuited or should continue;
- Does runtime dispatch occur before or after the return.

The three points here are observation points, not conclusions about an order that has already been established. The material does not provide specific hook names, caller examples, or stable output, so do not write a fabricated execution chain. The correction in MDX-216 has already flagged this gap; continuing to add "usually this first, then that" would only replace the old judgment with a new guess.

For records with an unmatched name, the most useful addition is not whether the path exists, but whether the name is declared as a public export by the export map. For return-point records, the most useful addition is not to prove once again that runtime can load it, but to determine whether any subsequent hook exists after the return. When each of the two record types is missing one piece, each must stop independently; success in one type cannot substitute for the other.

## Review excerpts and what is still only on paper

The two card records from the year 2025 left the page with two traces pointing in opposite directions but able to coexist: MDX-201 still says that one point about `export-map JSX resolution` is unconfirmed; MDX-216 points out that, in the loader and runtime dispatch sections, Node loader hook ordering is still unconfirmed. The former calls for continued investigation into name resolution; the latter prevents dispatch from being treated as an ordering conclusion. They are not duplicate descriptions of the same task.

The review feedback that was retained can be compressed into one sentence: do not use path reachability in place of a public export, and do not use one dispatch in place of hook-order evidence. The first half has already been incorporated into the current decision, while the second remains an open item. The open item is not a new proposal, nor is it a request to expand this page into a runtime design; it merely marks the edge in the decision record that remains unresolved.

The presence of DOC-12 also serves as a meeting-style boundary reminder: the short-circuit module return and this page's hook return point may appear within the same sequence of adjacent calls, but the structured reasons for the interface return are handled by DOC-12. If structured runtime causes appear during a cross-check, follow the navigation to the adjacent documentation; do not duplicate the interface contract here.

This page preserves only a limited record of the meeting: it records only the boundaries established by the split, without expanding the discussion into sentence-by-sentence minutes. For name resolution, the assessment concerns public exports; for hook ordering, it concerns direct observations of ordering. This distinction is enough to explain why the old paragraphs were discarded, and also why ordering remains unresolved.

## Appendix of old examples: still useful, but do not copy verbatim

### Old example A: treating a path as an export

```text
Name does not match the export map
→ Construct a filesystem path
→ Path exists
→ Continue loading the JSX runtime
```

This old example is retained in full because it explains why the `path` import was initially given too much weight. It is now **no longer applicable**. A path can exist, but that still does not mean it is a public export; continuing along this chain would reproduce the early misreading.

### Old example B: inferring order from a single dispatch

```text
runtime dispatch succeeds
→ Assume the loader hook order is as expected
```

This old example was not deleted because it is one of the reasons Node loader hook ordering has remained unresolved for so long. It only shows that an observation was overinterpreted, and cannot serve as a verification step. Following the MDX-216 correction, this example should be marked **subsequently overturned**.

### Old example C: looking only at the file header

```text
See the packages/loader/lib/index.js import
→ Attribute all resolution and execution decisions to this file
```

This example has not been judged entirely wrong. The file header is indeed an entry-point clue, but an "entry-point clue" is not the same as "all decisions". This page continues to reference it only for navigation to direct dependencies and local code, without elevating it into an explanation of the project's end-to-end flow.

The distinction between old example A and old example B should also be preserved. A mistakes path reachability for a name being exported, while B mistakes a single dispatch for execution order. They occur in adjacent loader contexts, but require different corrections. Merging the two examples would once again obscure the boundary between export map and hook ordering.

## Adjacent issues not yet split off

One point in `Node loader hook ordering` remains unconfirmed. No hook names, example return values, caller results, or reproducible failure output have been provided at this point, so an ordering table cannot be filled in here. If material is provided next time, it should at least make it possible to distinguish between: name resolution being complete but the hook order being unknown, or name resolution itself still having branches with no match; the two must no longer be grouped under a single "loader failure" label.

`export-map JSX resolution` should also not treat all related issues as complete just because the current position is now clear. The records for MDX-201 explicitly leave one point unconfirmed. The current decision addresses the relationship between public exports and fallback to unpublished paths; it does not automatically resolve every export-map branch, nor does it automatically provide examples of lookup misses. Leaving this gap here is more accurate than inventing a result.

If the loader side supplies additional material later, the most useful items would be two types of local artifacts: one result where processing can continue with a public name and one result where the name is not found; and an example that distinguishes the hook return from the runtime dispatch location. These serve name resolution and ordering assessment respectively, and the same successful record cannot provide both kinds of proof.

## Boundaries of the current decision

The only settled part is the approach to name resolution: public export-map names are the basis for determining the JSX runtime exports, and unpublished filesystem paths are not used as an automatic fallback. This boundary is sufficient to correct the earlier records and to let readers start checking from `packages/loader/lib/index.js`.

The part that remains undecided is Node loader hook ordering. The page will not gloss over it with a generalization such as "the loader and runtime dispatch are already fixed," nor will it transplant the short-circuit module return topic from DOC-12 into a conclusion about ordering here. Once direct local observations are available, they will be added in a later version; until then, both the old paragraphs and the traces of corrections will remain.

This is also the final shape of this legacy record: an old assessment that placed too much weight on paths at the beginning, a review that separated name resolution from execution order in the middle, and card counterexamples and a correction regarding dispatch later on, with the current position limited to public exports that can be confirmed.

- Return the module result only after confirming that the runtime has provided the JSX boundary.
- Do not use short-circuit as the default path for all JSX requests.

# MDX-3.0 Runtime Interface Proposal

Both investigations start at `script/jsx-loader.js`, but one asks when a module can be handed directly to the runtime, while the other asks what can still be retained after runtime execution fails. Tying them to the same switch makes the later samples hard to explain.

The dependencies directly visible in the file at this point are:

```js
import fs from 'node:fs/promises'
import {fileURLToPath} from 'node:url'
import {transform} from 'esbuild'
```

These three imports show that the review cannot focus only on return values. Path conversion and transform calls may both occur during normal processing; whether to enter the fast path must be determined using the JSX boundary provided by the call, not the file extension or whether a single transformation succeeded.

## Revised Trial Scope

Start by keeping two types of input: calls where the runtime has already provided the JSX boundary, and calls that still require loader processing. For the former, check whether the returned module can be used downstream; for the latter, check whether the call still goes through the existing processing. The goal here is not to force both sets of results into the same module shape, but to prevent the fast path from also cutting off normal processing.

Drop the original draft's claim that "successful samples are enough to prove that exceptions will be preserved". Successful calls have no runtime cause and cannot tell us where an exception cause will end up. For `structured runtime causes`, this round only requires checking failed calls: whether the structured result can still point to the cause that occurred at runtime, or whether that cause has already been lost before the return. The two outcomes correspond to different interface commitments and cannot be inferred from what the module returns.

## Options Still Being Compared

**Return directly based on the boundary condition.** This keeps the return decision local; the caller only needs to take this branch when it already has the JSX boundary. The risk is applying the condition too broadly, so normal requests also lose their existing processing.

**Always go through processing, then let the runtime consume the result.** This avoids the branch-identification problem, but does not address the fast-path return this trial is meant to verify, and would move the return point from the loader to a later stage.

The choice between these two options does not settle how exception causes are handled. The original cause could be retained for the structured result to reference, or the cause could be restructured at the interface boundary; the available material is not enough to choose. The review record needs to make clear both which side's boundary the failed call used and whether the final observation was the original exception or a wrapped cause.

If calls with a boundary already provided still need full processing to produce a usable module, the fast-path return is not viable; if calls without a boundary enter the same return branch, stop the trial immediately. Next time, add only the actual results for these two branches; do not expand this into an overall proposal for runtime error formats.

# MDX-3.0 Runtime Interface Proposal

This proposal originally framed the problem as "one fewer processing pass, while preserving exceptions." That wording led to a misreading: it seemed that as long as a module could be returned, information about runtime failures would naturally have somewhere to go too. The interface scope only became clear after a later review separated the two concerns.

The entry point for investigation is still `script/jsx-loader.js`. Three adjacent points are visible here: file reading, URL conversion, and `esbuild` conversion:

```js
import fs from 'node:fs/promises'
import {fileURLToPath} from 'node:url'
import {transform} from 'esbuild'
```

These are places to inspect the normal processing path, not conditions that trigger a fast-path return. An earlier draft used "the conversion did not error" as a rough test for whether an early return was possible; that test has been dropped. Successful conversion only shows that that processing pass completed. It does not show that the runtime already has the JSX boundary.

## The Original Combined Approach

The original proposal had two parts: when a call appeared to already meet the JSX conditions, have the loader return a module as early as possible; if the runtime then failed, the hope was that the same change would put the cause back into the result. It was concise to describe, but the downside was straightforward: successful cases could cover return timing, but not exception causes; failing cases, in turn, could not establish whether the module-return branch itself was correct.

A more aggressive alternative was also listed at the time: send all JSX requests through the fast-return path first, then let the runtime decide whether to do additional processing. This alternative was not pursued. It substituted "the request will eventually use JSX" for "the call has already supplied the boundary," leaving no place for work that should have been done by the loader. This conclusion did not come from a particular exception case, but from the fact that these are not the same condition.

Another earlier idea was to make the runtime cause a fixed part of the module return value. That is not being adopted either. Whether a module returns early and what structure preserves runtime exceptions are two distinct interface concerns; binding them together would force normal returns to carry failure semantics that do not belong to them.

## Current Trial Scope

This stage only covers confirming the fast-return conditions and keeping them independently checkable:

> The loader returns a short-circuited module when the runtime entry has already supplied the JSX boundary.

This statement sets two limits. First, the returned object is a short-circuited module; this does not change all loader calls to return directly. Second, the prerequisite is that the runtime entry has already supplied the JSX boundary; calls without that prerequisite cannot use this branch. During implementation review, first look for the boundary input at the runtime entry, then inspect the loader's return decision based on that input. Do not infer whether the boundary exists from the return value of `transform`.

Only two sets of minimal calls need to be kept in the trial record. In one set, the runtime entry supplies the JSX boundary; observe whether the module returned by the loader can then be passed to the runtime. In the other set, that boundary is not supplied; observe whether the call still falls back to the existing processing. Both sets should have explicit call preconditions. Recording only "success" or "failure" is not specific enough, because it could refer to either the conversion result or the result of subsequent runtime execution.

The two sets are not required to produce identical output. The first is useful for confirming that the short-circuit condition has no additional dependencies; the second, for confirming that normal processing has not been dropped. If a call without the boundary enters the short-circuit branch, or a call with the boundary still has to complete the original processing to obtain a usable module, revert this adjustment and go back to confirming where the condition comes from, rather than continuing to patch the returned object.

## Handling Exception Causes Separately

`structured runtime causes` remains a check to run in parallel. It does not change the return conditions above and should not be used as a substitute signal for deciding whether short-circuiting applies. The cases to inspect are those where an exception occurs after the runtime has received the module: whether the structured result can still point to that runtime cause, and whether the cause has been dropped or turned into something unrecognizable at the interface boundary.

The previous version described "preserve the cause on failure" as though it were already implemented; it is now an item to confirm. The existing entry point can help with investigation on the loader side, but it cannot replace checking the runtime result. If the cause exists only during execution and does not appear in the structured result, decide separately how to preserve it; do not relax the test for the JSX boundary to fill this gap.

Two approaches have been considered. In the first, the structured result references the original runtime cause, allowing caller Fang Ke to use it to distinguish execution failures from module-processing failures. In the second, the cause is restructured at the interface boundary, retaining only stable structured fields. The cost of the former is that caller Fang Ke can access the original object; the cost of the latter is that the relationship between the cause and the original exception needs additional explanation. The available material does not provide enough results to choose between them, so this is not being written up as a release commitment in this round.

## Exit Criteria and Remaining Questions

The exit criteria for this trial are narrow: short-circuiting occurs only when the runtime entry has supplied the JSX boundary; calls without the boundary retain the original processing; and successful-return cases do not obscure the need to check runtime causes. Once the first two are confirmed, the module-return work can be closed out independently. The third still requires actual results from failing calls; interface wording cannot substitute for them.

The unanswered question is which interface layer will ultimately preserve structured runtime causes, and whether callers receive the original cause or a restructured cause. This question remains part of the runtime-result review; `script/jsx-loader.js` serves only as the entry point for checking the return conditions and adjacent points in the normal processing path.

# MDX Runtime Diagnostics Troubleshooting Tree

This page did not originally start from a complete case. The old paper entry point contained only `docs/_asset/editor.jsx`, along with the four troubleshooting terms `runtime`, `production`, `jsx`, and `development`. What can be confirmed from the file header is as follows:

```js
import {compile, nodeTypes, run} from '@mdx-js/mdx'
import {createStarryNight} from '@wooorm/starry-night'
import sourceCss from '@wooorm/starry-night/source.css'
import sourceJs from '@wooorm/starry-night/source.js'
```

This file is recorded in the index as an existing jsx module, for code reading and checking historical behavior. It is an actual, accessible page entry point, with imports for compilation, node types, execution functions, and syntax-highlighting resources visible alongside it. The old records point here using issue names and call names, but do not identify the file location as the home of the implementation. The file header can help reproduce the entry point; it does not itself retain call results showing condition selection or diagnostic numbers.

## The First Sheet Beside the Entry Point

The 2023-03-20 approach first checks the pre-call state, then separates `compile` and `run`. The tree in that version was very short:

```text
Start
└─ Check the pre-call state
   ├─ runtime / production
   │  └─ Check whether there are visible changes after execution
   └─ runtime / development
      └─ Check whether there are visible changes after execution
```

These two are action branches, not rules that had already been proven at the time. The first draft treated production as the more likely path, with only "page entry points are usually like this" written beside it. It did not say whether the caller explicitly passed in conditions, nor did it retain both success and failure results. If someone had followed this tree all the way through at the time but ended up with only a screenshot of the page, they still would not know whether the position numbers appeared during compilation, at runtime, or at the page display stage.

The old page put `numeric diagnostic locations` at the end, as though it were a formatting issue. This placement preserves the blind spots from that time: there were no results from successful calls, no verbatim failure output, and no indication of whether the two calls used the same input. Unchanged numbers do not establish that position calculation is stable; not seeing numbers does not establish that no diagnostics were generated.

## Actions in the Margins of the On-Call Page

The later on-call addendum did not start by changing the old tree, but instead wrote more detailed actions beside it. Change only one condition per check, keeping the input and the remaining call options identifiable. First save the pre-call state, then check whether `compile` completes. After `compile` returns, first save the returned object and visible diagnostics, and do not simply mix the results together because the next step usually leads into `run`.

Commonly missing items in the field are:

```text
Input: to be retained
Changed item: runtime / development (choose one)
compile: success / failure (to be filled in)
run: success / not reached (to be filled in)
Visible changes: to be filled in
```

This small table is not a release checklist. It only separates three easily confused states: failure had already occurred before compilation; compilation completed but execution was not reached; execution was reached but there was no visible change. In the first case, stop at the failed step and save the original input and output. In the second case, save the returned object and the reason for stopping, without filling in execution results. Only in the third case should you compare the object passed to `run`, the condition values and the final result displayed on the page.

If the caller changed both `runtime` and `development`, this review cannot establish which change caused the difference. If the caller did not record the condition field, recording "unconfirmed" is more accurate than choosing a branch based on the text in the file. Without the pre-call state, do not use the current result on the page as the baseline either.

## The first unsuccessful troubleshooting approach

One investigation started by looking at the numeric positions on the editor page, then went back to look for the compilation return value. The numbers on the page stood out, so the initial working assessment was that the issue was in the editor display layer, and the recommendation was to check page rendering first. This sequence did not record which step had failed, nor did it establish that the object displayed on the page was the object generated by this call.

A later review labeled this passage "Later overturned: the generating layer cannot be determined solely from the numeric positions on the page". The old paragraph was not deleted, because it did record why the page was checked first at the time; the follow-up action only pointed forward to starting with the pre-call state and the original diagnostics. If only a screenshot is available, without the original failure output, the screenshot is still a clue from the incident, but it cannot by itself show which layer generated the position numbers.

The failed attempt also exposed a more specific gap: there were only failure samples, with no success samples. This left two possible meanings for "the numbers did not change", one being that both failures displayed the same position, and the other being that one of the attempts never reached the step that produces diagnostics. The old record did not distinguish between the two. During follow-up investigation, successful calls must also have a row; if a successful call has no numbers, explicitly record that no numbers were observed, rather than treating a blank as a zero value.

## A side note from a review

The year-end review in 2023 did not request that `docs/_asset/editor.jsx` be expanded into a complete call chain. The feedback focused on two gaps: the old page rushed through the default conditions; the original values of the position numbers were missing. The side note said, first confirm whether the caller explicitly requested `development`, then discuss the choice of `runtime`; do not treat `production` in a filename or on the page as evidence of behavior.

This side note did not rewrite the old passage above, so the page still shows both the old assessment and the later reminder. When reconstructing the historical situation, the old assessment belongs to its point in time; when conducting a new investigation, start with the caller state required by the side note. Do not simply copy the old paragraph and skip the side note.

The review also pointed out that the success and failure records must be traceable to the same input. It did not require writing a sample for every combination, nor is there supporting material for expanding this page into a complete compatibility matrix. The only thing that can be confirmed is the recording order: first save the input and conditions, then save the step results, and finally record the visible location.

## What changed in the second review

2024-03-21's review changed the tree from grouping by environment name to grouping by step:

```text
State before the call
├─ compile not completed
│  ├─ Failure output present: retain input, conditions, and location; stop
│  └─ No failure output: the observed state is incomplete; stop; do not fill in the run result
└─ compile completed
   ├─ run not entered: record the returned object and reason for stopping; stop
   └─ run entered
      ├─ Visible result present: then compare changes in conditions
      └─ No visible result: retain the empty result; do not assign a cause
```

This change corrected the action order; it did not prove that a particular filename corresponds to a particular actual condition, nor that a numeric position is necessarily produced by a particular function. The old sentence "no explicit development means production" remains, but it has been marked as unconfirmed later and can no longer be used as the starting point for troubleshooting.

The review also retained a concrete stopping point: if `compile` succeeds but does not enter `run`, the lack of a page change cannot be used to show that the run conditions did not take effect. Conversely, if it has already entered `run` but the page has no result, do not immediately return to the editor display layer; first retain the passed-in object, the state before the call, and the empty result. The three phenomena are adjacent, but they cannot substitute for one another.

This version can cite DOC-14 as a guide to adjacent compatibility records. DOC-14 does not provide evidence here for the condition determination or location numbers; the entry points and historical materials for the two pages still need to be considered separately. At present, no content from any later cards has been backfilled into this 2024 record.

## Items not pursued after the meeting

The meeting addressed the troubleshooting order for condition selection and diagnostic locations, but did not continue expanding on all imported symbols. The following issues therefore remain in the margin:

- The actual locations where `nodeTypes` is used in this entry point are not detailed on this page.
- The relationship between `createStarryNight` and the two source resources is visible only at the imports, with no call sites added.
- There has been no item-by-item comparison to check whether the numbers in the failure diagnostics come from the same object.
- There is no material confirming whether the page might still display old results when `run` has not been run.
- Whether the revision containing the old entry point covers the later entry-point changes was not investigated further on this page.

These are not new conclusions. They explain why the troubleshooting tree stopped early when output was missing. Writing further would present direct import relationships as runtime behavior, and page results as the location where diagnostics are generated.

## Correction log: first challenge the old assumption with a counterexample

The focused review in 2025 began by asking about a counterexample: if the caller explicitly requests `development`, would the old passage still treat production as the path? The old passage could not answer, because it recorded only the filename and the initial guess, not what the caller requested. So "production is the default" is no longer the starting point for troubleshooting, and the starting point is now to check whether the caller made an explicit request and what condition information this call actually left behind.

This is not an attempt to recast the old page as a new guide. The old passages, the old tree, and the unsuccessful troubleshooting methods remain above, along with the reasons; the correction only points forward to the new branches. Anyone who copies only "try production first" from the old page will still skip the pre-call state, which is exactly the historical trace this legacy record needs to preserve.

The correction regarding position numbers is also very limited. The numbers themselves are not evidence of the generation layer. Successful and failed calls must be recorded separately; each record must at least state whether the input was the same, whether the call passed through `compile`, whether it entered `run`, and whether position numbers were ultimately displayed. If any of these items is missing, it only indicates that the record of the situation is incomplete, not which layer performs the position calculation.

## Current verification approach

The production JSX condition is selected unless development is explicitly requested by the caller.

This statement appears in the current section near the end, and the earlier assumptions do not disappear as a result. What it changes is the troubleshooting order: first confirm whether the caller explicitly requested `development`; if there was no explicit request, check the actual result corresponding to the production JSX condition; if there was an explicit request, save both the request itself and the final visible result. Do not treat the file location of `docs/_asset/editor.jsx` as the source of this determination.

Proceed through the troubleshooting tree for the observed situation as follows:

```text
First save the pre-call state
├─ caller explicitly requested development
│  ├─ compile failed
│  │  └─ save the raw failure output and numeric locations, then stop
│  └─ compile succeeded
│     ├─ run was not entered
│     │  └─ save the return object and the reason for stopping
│     └─ run was entered
│        └─ save the visible result, then compare it with samples where it was not requested
└─ caller did not explicitly request development
   ├─ visible result with production JSX conditions
   │  └─ record the conditions and result; do not alter the input
   ├─ failure diagnostics only
   │  └─ save the original failure text and position numbers
   └─ no visible result
      └─ stop at what was recorded on site; do not infer the conditions from the page output
```

"not explicitly requested" does not mean the caller necessarily passed an empty value. It only means this record does not contain enough information to prove that an explicit request was made. If the call record has no condition field, stop at the gap; do not fill it in using the `production` or `development` text in the file.

## Field notation for numeric positions

Record the successful and failed calls separately. If the successful call has no diagnostic numbers, also write "no numbers seen," and note whether it passed through `compile` and `run`. For the failed call, retain the original input, the step where the failure occurred, and whether the page ultimately displayed numbers.

```text
Successful call
- whether caller explicitly requested development: to be verified
- compile: to be filled in
- run: to be filled in
- numeric diagnostic locations: none seen / to be filled in

Failed call
- same input: yes / no / unknown
- stop position: before compile / after compile / after run / unknown
- original diagnostic: paste the original text
- numeric diagnostic locations: paste the original value
```

If the inputs to the two calls differ, do not compare the position numbers yet. If the failed call has only a screenshot and no original diagnostic, retain the screenshot and the gap; do not transcribe the numbers in the screenshot as confirmed return values. If the successful call did not enter the run step, it cannot be used to prove the result of the run conditions.

If both calls entered `compile`, still record the return objects separately; do not record only "compile succeeded." If one path stops after `compile`, while the other path does not show a page change until after `run`, they are not a comparison at the same stage. If the page displays an old result, the current material cannot prove that the old result came from this call; record this as unknown for now.

## Using the old tree today

This page has been referenced many times, and the old tree has not been deleted. When you find an old section, first distinguish whether you are reconstructing the assessment from the year 2023 or handling the current situation. When reconstructing the old assessment, you may see the statement "production by default", but you must also note the unconfirmed marker that follows it; when handling the current situation, start directly from the pre-call state, not from the old conclusion.

If the symptom concerns the position displayed on the page, first check whether `compile` and `run` are from the same run. If the only symptom is a change in the position numbers, save the numbers and check both the success and failure records. If the symptom is a mismatch in condition selection, first check whether the caller explicitly requested `development`. These three entry points are close together, but each needs to answer a different question.

With only a file path and no call result, this page can only support tracing back to the entry point: inspect the imports at the top of the file and nearby objects, record the revision context, then stop. You cannot infer conditional behavior directly from a path. With only a page screenshot and no raw output, you can keep the screenshot as a clue, but do not treat it as a returned object or a failure diagnosis. With only failure samples and no success samples, you can describe the failure symptoms, but not how the numbers behave in normal calls.

## Old Appendix Still Retained

```text
runtime
  production? try first
  development? try next
check the result on the jsx page first
numeric positions seem to be an editor issue
```

These shorthand notes retain the original reasoning and no longer serve as the current sequence. They have no caller, `compile`, `run`, or success samples, so they can only be used to identify the old situation. Another old example was to trace back along the production path upon seeing production text on the page; this practice has since been abandoned. Filenames, import names, and page displays can only serve as nearby clues and cannot replace call records.

The appendix has not been deleted because old links still lead to this entry point. Readers who need to reconstruct the early troubleshooting can see how it prioritized page symptoms; readers handling new anomalies should return to the current tree below. These two uses cannot be merged into a single conclusion.

## Stop Conditions and Open Items

- No pre-call state: stop, do not compare conditions.
- No raw failure output: save the available screenshots and mark the gap, do not infer the source of the numbers.
- No confirmation of whether `compile` or `run` was entered: stop at the corresponding node.
- Success and failure use different inputs: stop comparing position numbers.
- Only a file path, with no call result: only trace back to the entry point, do not draw behavioral conclusions.
- Only page results, with no corresponding returned object: do not confirm the generation layer.

What remains unconfirmed is how `numeric diagnostic locations` appears in successful calls, and whether the numbers from failed calls are generated together with the same diagnostic object. - Assert on the user-visible result produced by `compile`. This requires more changes, but preserves the actual usage boundary of pragma scope.
- Keep only the investigation entry point initially and add the regression back once the implementation location is fully clear. This avoids writing the test in the wrong place, but leaves no behavioral protection.

# pragma Scope Decision Record

The May version left just one small decision: do not use internal helper function names as proof of pragma scope. At the time, the available material was insufficient to describe the full implementation path for pragma, and there was no reason to turn a syntax test file into a map of implementation ownership. Its value lay in making regression tests focus on results users can see, rather than on internal names the tests happened to be able to access.

The later review again started from `packages/mdx/test/syntax.js`. The direct connections visible in this file at the frozen revision are as follows:

```js
import assert from 'node:assert/strict'
import {test} from 'node:test'
import {compile} from '@mdx-js/mdx'
import {h} from 'hastscript'
```

This import block does not provide the semantics of pragma scope, nor does it say where a particular pragma should be inherited. It only provides a practical starting point: assertions, a test framework, `compile`, and the `h` used when constructing syntax trees are already present together here. Therefore, when investigating a regression related to syntax results, it is reasonable to start by looking at how the existing tests express their assertions here; claiming that a particular module owns the pragma implementation, however, requires further verification by following references. These two things cannot be collapsed into "the tests are here, so the implementation is here too".

## Initial Options and Outcome

The choice at the time was not "whether to write tests", but "what exactly the tests should substantiate". There were reasons to retain each of the three options:

| Option | Benefit at the time | Reason for rejection or retention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assert internal helper function names | Small changes, with familiar names that could be located quickly during investigation | Names change during cleanup and cannot express the externally visible results of pragma scope |
| Assert user-visible results after `compile` | Assertions are close to actual usage, and internal renaming should not change their meaning | The expected visible difference must first be stated clearly; a vague "it compiled" is not a substitute |
| Record only `syntax.js` as the entry point, without adding a regression test yet | Avoids committing to an incorrect assertion before the relationships are clear | Recording an entry point does not itself protect behavior, and the next change could repeat the same kind of omission |

The second option was selected. Here, "user-visible" does not mean that tests must expose every internal intermediate state; it means that the results described by the assertions must not depend on internal helper function names. The first option was not retained as a basis for regression tests; the third serves only as navigation. This distinction is the decision recorded on this page.

An early claim risked conflating things: since `syntax.js` imports `h`, it should be possible to characterize pragma issues directly at the tree-construction layer. That claim was not retained after review. `h` is a directly visible dependency of that file; beyond that, this page has no evidence that it is the point where pragma scope is defined, its sole execution point, or its boundary of responsibility. It is fine to treat it as a neighboring component to investigate; it is not fine to rewrite the scope of the requirements on that basis.

## Boundaries Covered by This Decision

Here, pragma scope refers to a usage boundary that needs protection through repository regression tests, not a specification redefining pragma syntax. The decision covers the level of assertions and the starting point for verification:

1. New or adjusted regression tests should assert user-visible results, not internal helper function names.
2. Start the review from the existing test connections around `packages/mdx/test/syntax.js`, focusing on how `compile` is used to produce results that can be asserted.
3. The fact that `assert`, `test`, `compile`, and `h` appear together is used only to organize this inspection, not interpreted as a complete call chain.
4. Do not concentrate all responsibility for pragma scope, its implementation, or subsequent changes in this file merely because the test filename contains syntax.

The second point especially needs to be explicit. `compile` is a directly visible import in this file, so it is a suitable nearby target for behavioral assertions; however, "compilation succeeds" is still too weak on its own. If a test only proves that a call did not throw, without showing what difference pragma scope made to the final visible result, it may still give a misleading green light after internal paths change. Regression expectations should be expressed in terms of results, not as guesses about whether a helper with a particular name was called.

This also explains why the approach "first locate every implementation site, then decide where to put the test" was not selected. Establishing implementation ownership and protecting behavior proceed at different paces. The former requires incremental verification by following references; the latter can first pin down an externally visible result within the existing `compile` test connections. As long as the assertion does not pretend to know internal paths that have not yet been confirmed, this ordering does not elevate a provisional investigative judgment into an architectural conclusion.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> syntax_js: Review from the syntax test entry point
    syntax_js --> helper_name: Internal-name assertion
    syntax_js --> visible_result: Compilation-result assertion
    helper_name --> rejected: Not a basis for regression tests
    visible_result --> adopted: Retain user-visible results
    adopted --> counterexample: Check coverage with a counterexample
```

The states in the diagram are not a runtime flow. The diagram only records how this decision places a visible test entry point, two assertion approaches, and a counterexample added later on the same line of reasoning.

## Later Counterexample Record

`MDX-211` became a referenceable navigation card in September. The observation recorded when the card was created was "pragma scope integrated into everyday workflows", and the retained to-do requirement was "add a repository regression test for 'pragma scope' that asserts user-visible results rather than internal helper function names". This gave the May choice a clear follow-up target: regression tests are not there to endorse the test file's internal structure, but to cover results that can surface in everyday use.

The activity history from the same day also recorded `counterexample_added`. The record did not spell out the counterexample's input, output, or specific expression, so this page does not fill in a seemingly precise example. What can be confirmed from it is that the review no longer stopped at the original positive assessment; a counterexample had been added to test whether the earlier assertions had drawn the scope boundary too broadly. The existence of a counterexample does not automatically establish that all neighboring scenarios are covered, nor does it turn unrecorded implementation details into established facts.

That afternoon, the card's assignee changed once. The recorded reason was straightforward: the previous assignee had only helped with triage, and the item was returned to the actual maintainer. This change does not alter the May choice of test focus, but it clarifies how follow-up work should be handled. During triage, `syntax.js`, `compile`, and the existing assertions can help quickly narrow down the issue; deciding test expectations, maintaining regression tests, and interpreting the counterexample should be carried forward by the actual maintainer. Someone who participated in the initial diagnosis cannot automatically be regarded as the long-term owner of pragma scope.

The counterexample also changed the minimum requirements for "behavioral assertions". The original instruction merely said not to assert internal names, which could still be misread as allowing any outer-layer string to suffice. It should now be understood at two levels: first, assertions must target user-visible results; second, they must distinguish the boundary revealed by the counterexample, rather than merely prove a convenient happy path. Which helper functions this boundary passes through in the source code is not covered by this decision.

## Handling Neighboring Interface Topics Separately

DOC-22 discusses JSX option isolation. Like this page, it is part of the MDX-3.0 interface work, so navigation to the related documentation is retained; however, the two subjects cannot share the same conclusion merely because both are close to JSX or compilation options. The pragma scope regression decision focuses on the results pragma leaves in everyday use, while the interface review for JSX option isolation should be supported by its own option boundaries and results for callers.

Therefore, this page does not frame the assessment of JSX option isolation as a premise for pragma, nor does it use pragma's counterexample in place of the interface evidence on the other page. When the two need to be read side by side, DOC-22 only provides an entry point to the neighboring topic, not evidence for this decision.

Likewise, having `hastscript`'s `h` and `@mdx-js/mdx`'s `compile` appear together in a test file does not mean that the two have the same responsibilities in every scenario. What is actually settled here is how to write the regression tests: use the existing syntax test connections to help produce observable compilation results, then use those results to support the protection goal for pragma scope.

## Decision Ledger

| Item | Conclusion |
| --- | --- |
| What the regression tests assert | User-visible results |
| What is not evidence of requirements | Internal helper function names |
| First entry point for repository verification | `packages/mdx/test/syntax.js` |
| Directly visible compilation API | `compile` |
| Review material added in September | One recorded counterexample |
| Ownership of follow-up work | Returned to the actual maintainer |

This ledger deliberately does not give the contents of the counterexample or expand the test file's direct dependencies into a module diagram. Those details are not elaborated in the existing records. Leaving those gaps is more useful than stitching `h`, `compile`, or file paths into an apparently complete implementation story.

One question still needs to be answered in the concrete regression change: how to express the visible distinction required by the counterexample in a way that both covers everyday use of pragma scope and avoids treating internal naming or incidental formatting as part of the interface. This question does not revoke the choice already made; it constrains the form of the final assertion. As long as the regression tests continue to use user-visible results as their standard and can still distinguish the added counterexample, the decision in place since May has not been overturned by subsequent review.

# JSX Options Isolation Proposal

This round of API review is initially narrowed to the JSX configuration on the evaluate call. The existing investigation points to `packages/mdx/lib/util/resolve-evaluate-options.js` as the entry point; treat this as the initial verification point, without taking it as a conclusion about caller ownership.

One concern is that the JSX options processed for one call may affect the next call. There is not enough evidence yet to determine which layer the effect comes from: the input object itself may be mutated, or the processed object may continue to be used later in the flow. These two cases must be handled separately.

Three approaches have been considered:

- Copy the entire options object before each call, then process JSX on the copy.
- Take only the portion required by JSX, and generate a derived configuration for this call.
- Continue reusing the original object, but restore the changes after the call ends.

The first is the most direct change, but it would obscure which fields actually belong to JSX; the third depends on restoration order, so it is not suitable as the first choice. Tentatively favor the second: put the isolation point at the option-processing step, while callers continue to pass options as before.

Two adjacent-call examples are still needed: one where the first call includes JSX configuration and the second does not; and one where the two calls include different JSX configurations. If both calls still get the same processed result, the issue cannot be attributed to the JSX field itself.

The rollback conditions are simple: if the derived configuration changes evaluate behavior unrelated to JSX, or if callers depend on object identity, stop pursuing this approach and go back to comparing against a full copy of the options. It has not yet been confirmed whether anyone depends on object identity.
