# JSX Option Isolation Proposal

The first draft focused on "do not reuse the JSX configuration", which was too broad. After review, the investigation still starts with `packages/mdx/lib/util/resolve-evaluate-options.js`, but the discussion is limited to the JSX portion of the evaluate options within a single normalization pass. This file is the current reference point for further investigation; whether other call paths exist cannot be inferred directly from the filename.

The scope of MDX-212 has been confirmed, but the card still has outstanding tasks to trigger differences using existing tests or examples and add coverage for uncovered user paths. This document retains a trial approach on the interface side, rather than rewriting the card's pending investigation items as completed conclusions.

## Narrowing the Scope After Review

Three things need to be distinguished.

First, whether the caller passes the same options object to two evaluate calls; this determines whether cross-call residue might be observed. Second, whether option normalization writes any JSX-related content; isolation has a concrete target only if writes occur. Third, whether subsequent code requires the original object back with the same identity; even if the field values are identical, replacing the object may change compatibility behavior.

The first draft collapsed these three things into a single "copy options" action, which was too coarse. We no longer recommend starting by changing the entire input. Copying everything may make the behavior appear stable, but it couples JSX isolation with the handling of other fields; if differences arise later, it will be hard to tell which part was protected.

Also, this proposal does not address Rollup's option forwarding. That boundary is tracked separately in DOC-23. Both areas involving options does not mean that forwarding rules and JSX normalization rules can be merged in the same place; this proposal only requires that the fix for JSX not be used to change the forwarding policy.

## Candidate Approaches

**Copy everything.** Copy the incoming options before each normalization pass, and fill in the JSX-related values on the copy. This is easy to try, and calls will not directly share the normalized copy. The cost is an overly broad scope: non-JSX fields will also be moved into a new object, and if an adjacent path relies on object identity or reads the original object later, this approach will introduce changes unrelated to the problem. It is suitable for comparison, not for immediate adoption as the interface strategy.

**Derive a JSX configuration.** Preserve the options supplied by the caller, and collect the parts that JSX needs to read or supplement into a derived configuration for a single call. This makes the isolation point clear: the original input still belongs to the caller, while the normalized JSX state belongs only to the current evaluate call. What needs confirmation is not "whether it can be copied", but which values truly belong to JSX and which are simply ordinary options for the same evaluate call. This approach is the currently recommended direction for the trial.

**Modify in place, then restore.** Record the JSX-related fields on entry, then restore them at the end. This appears to preserve object identity, but restoration depends on running on every exit path; exceptions, early returns, or nearby asynchronous operations all increase the chance of missing restoration. There is no evidence that the current path has these exits, nor is there any need to design the approach as a restoration protocol just to retain this assumption, so it will not be pursued further.

The review also retained a counterexample: even if the JSX configurations differ between two calls, a difference in results does not necessarily indicate shared state, as long as the second call reads input freshly supplied by the caller. In contrast, a sequence in which the first call includes JSX configuration and the next call does not is more useful, because it checks whether the later call unexpectedly inherits values normalized by the earlier call. This counterexample only defines the observation order; it does not assume that residual state already exists in the current implementation.

## Planned Trial

The trial will not change how callers pass arguments. First, construct a derived JSX configuration for the current call at the option normalization point, then have the existing evaluate path read it. The original options should not serve as the container for normalization results.

The comparison should retain at least two sequences:

1. The first call includes JSX configuration, and the second call does not.
2. Both calls include JSX configuration, but the configurations differ.

The first sequence checks whether a call using defaults inherits state from the previous round; the second checks whether the later call still reads its own input. Both should start with existing tests or examples, rather than creating a new test framework disconnected from the actual entry point. If the existing examples cannot express adjacent calls, first record the gap back in MDX-212, rather than treating "not reproduced" as successful isolation.

A narrower compatibility cost also needs attention: if options outside JSX are read from the same normalization object, establishing the derivation boundary too early may cause those reads to lose their original adjacency. Therefore, the trial code should not split all of options into two parallel sets of objects; only move normalization results confirmed to belong to JSX out of the original input. This record does not currently provide a fixed list of fields that meet this condition.

## Withdrawal and Open Items

The withdrawal conditions have been changed from the first draft's broad wording to three criteria: the derived configuration causes differences in non-JSX evaluate paths; a caller object whose identity must be preserved is replaced; or the two sequence examples cannot clarify the isolation boundary and instead only expose earlier input problems. If any criterion is met, stop treating the derived configuration as the default approach, first run a localized comparison using a full copy, then decide whether to retain the changes.

Still unconfirmed: whether callers reuse the same options object; whether there are other readers of the JSX normalization results; and which user paths described in MDX-212 are already covered by existing tests. The latter two items will determine the actual size of the derivation boundary.

The first draft's "restore after the call ends" approach is retained here as an abandoned candidate, no longer as an implementation recommendation. Its value is in showing that the intent at the time was to preserve object identity; after review, the restoration order itself would become a new interface burden.

# Rollup Option Forwarding Troubleshooting Tree

When you see "Rollup option forwarding", first treat it as a case label that still needs to be traced. What you need to find is the actual caller still using this phrase: which version it used, which entry point it went through, and what result it ultimately obtained. The issue name itself does not provide these three layers of information, and the filename cannot substitute for them.

Start assessing the case with this tree:

```text
Issue name / call name
  └─ Can it point to a caller that is still in use?
       ├─ No: retain the original label, stop at locating the caller
       └─ Yes: record the actual version, entry point, and current result
             ├─ All four items available: continue checking where options are passed
             ├─ Version missing: stop comparing the old and current entry points
             ├─ Entry point missing: stop determining which path was taken
             └─ Result missing: only log the item for verification, do not attribute a cause
```

## Identify the Entry Point First

The old troubleshooting materials point the issue name and call name to `packages/mdx/lib/util/resolve-file-and-options.js`. This path can still be used as a starting point for the search, but it only tells you that the old record used this search location. What can currently be checked directly at the top of the file is:

```js
import {VFile} from 'vfile'
import {md} from './extnames.js'
```

First record the entry point reported by the caller exactly as provided, then compare it side by side with this path. If the names match, that only means the search direction is consistent; you still need the actual version and current result to determine whether this is still the working entry point. If the names differ, do not immediately record this as a forwarding failure either. Retain both entry points and continue confirming which one the caller actually went through.

`option` and `options` in the filename can only help with searching; their wording alone cannot establish that options are received, rewritten, or lost here. Likewise, the imports of `VFile` and `md` are facts about the local file, not proof of Rollup behavior. The old materials contain neither failure output that can be copied directly nor a complete call chain; do not add an unsourced chain here.

## After Finding the Caller

Once you have a matching caller, record four values first. The values must come from the same verification session; do not assemble a set using the version from an old screenshot, the entry point from the current page, and a result recalled from memory.

| Item | How to record it |
| --- | --- |
| Caller | The actual object or page name that can be linked to this issue label |
| Actual version | The version the caller was using at the time, preserving its original notation |
| Entry point | The entry point the caller actually went through |
| Current result | The result seen during verification, preserving the original description of normal or abnormal behavior |

Once all four items are available, return to `packages/mdx/lib/util/resolve-file-and-options.js` to inspect what the caller passes to the entry point and how options are specified near that entry point. Do not reverse the order: record the input first, then inspect the local code, and finally place the observations alongside the caller's result. This makes it clear exactly what was verified this time, without presenting "should be forwarded" as something that has already happened.

If the caller's result is normal, simply record "The result of this check is normal". The old version, old entry point, and current entry point may not belong to the same combination, so a single normal result is not enough to declare that the old issue is gone. If the result is abnormal, retain the observed abnormal behavior and the four identifying values; without a corresponding code snippet or output, do not write "the file swallowed the option".

## Branches for Missing Information

**Only an issue name or call name.** Retain the original label and this path, and stop at finding the caller. Do not infer module responsibility from the directory location of `resolve-file-and-options.js`, and do not interpret the imports at the top of the file as evidence of option forwarding.

**A caller is available, but no actual version.** You can record the object and entry point, but cannot compare the old record with the current result. An old link that opens does not mean it corresponds to the current version; keep it among the historical leads for now.

**A version is available, but no entry point.** Version information cannot prove that this file path was used. Do not automatically associate the version with the old path, and wait for the caller to provide the actual entry point.

**An entry point is available, but no current result.** This only indicates the search direction; do not write "recovered" or "still failing". If the result comes from an old screenshot or old link, retain the time context shown in the screenshot and keep it separate from the current verification.

**All four items are available, but no local snippet or output.** You can record the identifying information, but cannot infer what happened to a specific option from the filename, import names, or familiar Rollup behavior. What is missing is not a summary sentence, but direct material from this verification session.

## A Previously Blocked Verification

The navigation instructions in [MDX-213] are to find a caller still using this phrase and check the actual version, entry point, and current result. Historical activity at 2025-10-13 shows that reproduction moved to Blocked at the time because the read-only account was still awaiting approval; at 2025-10-14, it returned to To Do. What can be confirmed here is that the prerequisites for reproduction were not met in time; do not describe the status changes as meaning that the issue was reproduced, fixed, or that the behavior of a particular option was confirmed.

When the same situation recurs during verification, record "The read-only account has not yet been approved" as the blocker. Do not substitute a different set of accounts, another version, or a result recalled from memory. Even if approval is completed later, you must still obtain the actual version, entry point, and current result from the caller again; an approval outcome alone is not enough to conclude the behavior assessment. If there is no approval outcome, troubleshooting can stop at this branch, leaving the status unresolved.

This history also explains why the old records continued to contain only an entry point and no conclusion: what was missing at the time was the prerequisites for reproduction, not a code answer that could be inferred from the filename. Anyone revisiting the case should distinguish between "the path has been obtained" and "the caller's result has been observed".

## Boundaries for Recovery Actions

The first step you can take is to put the four identifying values provided by the caller and the file path in the same record. Then check only how options are actually specified in the current case, and paste the corresponding local code or result. If the two cannot be matched, stop at describing the discrepancy, and do not fill the gaps by modifying files, switching versions, or guessing about the adapter.

If the only material you have is an old link, first retain the version and entry point it points to. The fact that an old entry point opens does not mean the caller still enters there; the fact that an old result looks abnormal does not mean the same abnormal behavior still occurs now. If a new entry point appears, record the old and new entry points separately, and do not merge them into a single continuous call chain.

If you need to look back at reproduction progress in [MDX-213], use it only as a navigation entry point. The card history can show that approval for the read-only account once blocked reproduction; it cannot replace the caller's actual result. When returning to this page with related records, still start with the four identifying values.

## Stopping Points

- Only an issue name or call name: stop at locating the caller.
- Only able to open the file path: stop at finding the entry point, and do not attribute a cause to the behavior.
- An entry point but no version: do not compare the results from the two sets of entry points.
- A version but no current result: do not write a conclusion of recovery or failure.
- The read-only account is still not approved: record the blocker, and do not describe it as a reproduction result.
- All four items are available but no code snippet or output: record the scope of observation, and do not infer the behavior of a specific option.

The retained old entry point is the part of this material that remains useful; the old assessment should not be treated as the current standard. To continue verification, you must obtain the version, entry point, and result from the actual caller again.

# Alternative Approach Proposal for the Reference Site

The comparison at the time was between continuing the cleanup under `condition` and splitting `VFile` out on its own. Both approaches supported the access point for `mdx-documentation-portal`, but neither had entered a trial. The draft favored splitting out `VFile`, because the two parts had different failure exits in the existing material; keeping both under `condition` made it easy to treat different failure cases as one category in the records. This judgment was only an assumption in the proposal, not an implementation that had already been adopted.

The advantages of staying with `condition` were the small scope of changes and the ease of retaining the old entry point. The reference site's `docs` and `guide` entry points could continue to share the original organization method, without first changing the handling paths for release notes or outdated content. The cost was that the same place would have to handle two types of failure exit, making it hard to tell which part had gone wrong when reviewing the records later. If an entry-point failure left only `condition`, this draft could not determine from that whether the issue was in the reference content, entry-point organization, or adapter layer.

The benefit of splitting out `VFile` was to record the two types of failure exit separately, so the reference site's maintainers could later review the corresponding content by exit. It would also run into the boundary of `adapter` again: if the split-out object took responsibility for this boundary, existing calls Fang Ke might need adjustment; if the old entry point remained responsible for it, the split would change only recordkeeping and might not be worth the extra maintenance cost. The existing callers of `adapter` had not been verified at the time, so those relationships cannot be filled in here as established facts.

The proposed trial was limited to the reference site's entry points and their failure records, with no advance commitment to a new maintenance path. The review needed a contrasting input to observe each of the two types of failure exit and see whether they could still be distinguished; if the results were still mixed together in `condition`, the main rationale for the split would not hold. That validation window had not been completed at the time, and the handling of release notes and outdated content had not been settled alongside it. The exact content of the contrasting input, where it would be run, and the assessment record were all left open.

The rollback point was to be interpreted as narrowly as possible: if the split made callers harder to maintain, first roll back the newly added `VFile` branch; whether to restore only the old entry point had not been decided at the time. There were two different recovery scopes here: remove only the newly added branch, or revert the entry-point organization to the old approach as well. The draft did not have enough material to choose between them, so "restore the old entry point" cannot be written as a settled action.

No adoption record was produced for this approach; the earlier assessment and rollback conditions are retained here. If this is reopened, first answer two questions: who calls `adapter` now, and whether a rollback would restore only the old entry point. Until those are answered, do not present it as the current entry-point documentation. The reference site's working copy still corresponds to `docs/adj-mdx/proposals/unadopted-mdx-user-documentation-portal-approach.md`, and that project maintains the body and attachments; this path is an entry point to the material, not a cutover entry point that is already live.

# Migration of Old and New Entry Points on the Documentation Site

This index remains on the documentation site because an old entry point does not disappear just because the directory is renamed. The usage entry points formed by docs and guide have their own version notes and may also retain outdated content; they have independent schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria. This does not attempt to rewrite all historical pages using the same wording; it only lists the old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still in use that can already be identified within mdx-documentation-portal. Explanations that cannot be traced back continue to be marked outdated; do not fill them in using a directory organized later.

The entry-point material is still at `docs/adj-mdx/migration/current-entry-point-legacy-entry-point-migration-index.md`. This file is a visible locator in the documentation-site export; it does not mean that every explanation in it is still a current procedure. When someone reaches this page through an old link, check the status next to the entry first; old paragraphs without a status can only be understood according to their purpose when they were written.

## Indexing Conventions

Record each migration object separately; do not treat "the page can still be opened" and "the caller has switched to the replacement location" as the same thing. The old entry point records where people entered in the past; the replacement location records where people are currently intended to enter; the caller column records only people or pages confirmed to still use the old entry point. Version notes are listed separately because they often retain old names but may no longer point to an entry point that can still be used.

The recommended recording order is to first copy down the visible name of the old entry point on the documentation site, then record the replacement location, and finally add the caller. This is not for formatting the directory; it is so that rollback still makes it possible to determine what should be restored. If the old item is deleted before the replacement item is added, all that will be visible afterward is the new directory, and the original entry point and old version notes will be lost together.

```text
Old entry ──────> Existing documentation on the documentation site
   │                 │
   │ Keep rollback line    └─> Replacement location
   │                         │
   └─────────────────────────┘
             Confirmed callers migrate one by one
```

The two lines in the diagram intentionally do not merge at the replacement location. An old entry point being readable does not mean that it continues to carry new documentation; a replacement location having appeared does not mean that the old callers have finished migrating. "Complete" in the index should correspond only to confirmation from one specific caller, and should not be applied to the directory as a whole.

## Do Not Rush to Remove Old Entries

The past practice was to treat an old entry point as removable as soon as a replacement location appeared in guide. This later proved insufficient: the directory can show the new location, but it cannot indicate whether the old link is still being used or whether the old version notes still contain a valid way in. Therefore, retain the old entry point as a readable record until the caller has an explicit migration result.

Retention does not require continuing to maintain the old content. An old item can be marked outdated or can retain only a pointer to the replacement location; the key is not to make readers think that it never existed. In particular, if no corresponding replacement location or caller is found for an old name in the version notes, continue to treat it as outdated. It should not be rewritten as a seemingly complete new path.

The "current entry point" on the documentation site is also only the entry point seen by that migration record. Later page changes may already have altered the actual navigation, but this page does not backfill those changes. When someone needs to compare a later version, they should verify it separately from the current documentation-site entry point, then return to the old path retained here.

## The Split Decision Left by the First Version

The first version made a choice between `import` and `pragma`: one approach was to continue along `import` while retaining the old entry point, and the other was to split `pragma` out separately. The two failure exits visible at the time were different, so they were not written as one migration action. This judgment is retained here to explain why the index does not automatically merge entries based on similar names.

At that time, the split was not treated as the final plan. The current callers of `hook` had not been fully identified, and it had not been decided whether rollback should restore only the old entry point. The old draft's "inclination to split out `pragma`" was therefore only a working judgment at the time; it must not be used to infer that all entry points had been migrated in that way. This passage was not deleted when the index was later supplemented: it explains why some old paths still have a blank caller column beside them.

If similarly named entry points with different failure exits are encountered again, first record them separately in the old-path column, and decide whether to merge them only after both the callers and replacement locations can be matched. Conversely, do not assume that two entries have the same rollback method just because they both contain the same technical term.

## Migrating from the Old Entry Point to the Replacement Location

Before starting the migration, retain the pre-change route snapshot. The snapshot represents the entry-point relationship on the documentation site at that time, not a cleaned-up screenshot; it is used to restore the old entry point and to confirm exactly where a particular old explanation pointed. Then move one confirmed caller to the replacement location, while temporarily retaining the old entry point.

During the migration, verify only the actual result after that caller enters from docs or guide. The appearance of a replacement location in the directory, an updated page title, or an old explanation being marked outdated is not evidence that the migration is complete. What actually needs to be recorded is: where the caller originally entered from, where it was changed to, whether it can still find the required explanation after the change, and which old path should be restored if rolled back.

"Caller" is not counted here by the number of times it appears in the directory. The same old path may be referenced by different explanations, or there may be only one place that is still using it. The index does not count an unconfirmed reference as migrated; it is better to leave the item at "pending confirmation" than to mark it as switched over just to complete a batch of migrations.

After the replacement location appears, retain a rollback line beside the old path. Rollback does not mean re-editing a version note to explain the old entry point; it means restoring the previous entry-point relationship and then checking it once with the original caller. If the originally visible explanation still cannot be obtained after restoration, stop deleting old items and return to the route snapshot and old version notes for verification.

## Addendum on Exit Actions

Later exit work did not turn this index into the current release process. MDXA-008 records the arrangement for the original owner to review the exit action before expiration; as that card was progressed, the recorded observation was that the on-duty person's round had already been reviewed, but the exit entry point itself had not yet been tested. Therefore, "the on-duty person has already checked it" cannot be written as confirmation that the exit entry point has been verified, much less used as a reason to delete the old path.

MDXA-015 indicates that the old exit action still has route residue. When handling this residue, retain the pre-change route snapshot, then delete the operation pointing to the old exit action. This addendum resolves only the residual operation; it does not confirm on this page that all old entry points have completed migration. The card later received confirmation of responsibility; this still does not change the limitation in the preceding paragraph: when the entry point itself has not been tested, the index should retain its unconfirmed status.

Therefore, exit actions and ordinary entry-point migrations are kept separate here. Ordinary entry-point migration focuses on whether the caller reaches the replacement location; exit actions focus on whether the old route will still be triggered. The two may be located near the same documentation-site content, but restoration requires different objects. The former restores the old entry point; the latter depends on the pre-change route snapshot, and they cannot substitute for each other.

## Version Notes and Outdated Content

Old version notes are often used as entry-point documentation, which is also why the index retains them. If an old note can still help identify the path at that time, do not remove it directly just because it is outdated; simply note beside it that it cannot be traced back. Readers can use it to learn what the old entry point once served, but should not treat it as operating instructions for the replacement location.

Only explanations that can be traced back should be filled into the three columns for old entry point, replacement location, and caller. Explanations that cannot be traced back retain their existing outdated status; do not guess their new destination. The directory structure, page names, or subsequent version notes on the documentation site are not sufficient to prove that a new entry point has taken over an old explanation.

This is also why this page does not include every similar page. The value of the index is in distinguishing confirmed migration relationships from names left in history, not in providing a site-wide navigation map that merely looks orderly. If the original caller is found later, it can be added under the corresponding old path; if it is not found, the old explanation can simply remain in the outdated section.

## Recoverable Stop Points

Do not continue deleting old entry points in any of the following cases: the replacement location is only a new item in the directory; the caller has not been confirmed; the old version note has no corresponding entry point; or the exit entry point has not actually been tested. In that situation, retaining the old path, the pre-change route snapshot, and the existing version notes is more useful than adding a speculative migration conclusion.

Even after a confirmed caller has migrated over, do not immediately erase the old entry point from the index. First change it to a historical entry, retaining the replacement location and the confirmation result. That way, when someone returns with the old link next time, it will still be clear that this is a path that has been migrated away from, rather than a broken page with no known origin.

When restoring the old path, first restore the entry-point relationship according to the snapshot; do not overwrite the old notes with the current version notes. After restoration, check only whether the original caller can again find the content it originally saw; if it cannot, stop subsequent migration and record whether what is missing is the entry point, the explanation, or the caller confirmation. There is not enough material here to attribute all three types of problem to the same cause.

## Entry Points for the Handoff

MDXA-008 and MDXA-015 serve only as navigation to records related to exit actions. The former reminds readers that the exit entry point has not been tested; the latter corresponds to the route residue from the old exit action and retention of the snapshot. They cannot replace caller confirmation in the documentation site.

The field record for the current entry point can be linked to DOC-26; this page maintains only the index and rollback relationship from the old entry point to the replacement location. If the documentation site has a new entry-point change later, add a new record; do not overwrite the time context recorded here for `import`, `pragma`, `hook`, and the old route residue.

Still to be added are the current caller of `hook` mentioned in the first version, and whether that rollback restored only the old entry point. No confirmable record was found for either item, so continue to mark them beside the old judgment.
versions.change_summary: Add handling for leftover old routes, rollback, and outdated documentation

# Quality Signal Console Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the Quality Signal Console is stuck, start with the symptoms visible from the current entry point. Here, "stuck" includes: the second run or read does not produce a result for the current revision, the content before and after an exit action does not match, the standard entry point is denied access, and records exist but the first difference from the most recent known-good sample cannot be located within the project. These cases cannot all use the same recovery action.

First save the original input, the version used and the result first displayed. If the entry point provides a request/run id, retain it as well; when the standard entry point is denied access, also note where the denial occurred. Do not switch to an administrator identity first, and do not clear the cache first and then paste a green result back into the original record. Doing so conflates permissions problems and cache problems as the same kind of "recovered" state.

## Entry Point Tree

```text
Did the current entry point leave a raw record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Standard entry point denied access directly: save the denial location and request/run id
│  │  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner; do not substitute an administrator identity for the standard entry point
│  └─ No run or read records at all: collect additional data, then stop
└─ Yes
   ├─ Result for the current revision missing from the second run or read: preserve where it is missing
   │  └─ Only the final state remains: leave this field blank, do not infer the second result retroactively
   ├─ Current result appears once the cache is cold: retain both records from before and after the cache became cold
   │  └─ Exit action still displays the original result: go to the exit action branch
   └─ Can be compared with the most recent known-good sample
      ├─ First difference is still within esbuild-quality-signal: the maintainer on duty continues
      └─ Difference crosses a clearly defined interface: hand off to the interface owner with the raw records
```

The tree determines what material to obtain next, not what to name the cause in advance. Without raw records, the only thing that can be confirmed is "the current entry point did not leave enough content"; continuing to compare versions, directories or final displays will not recover the first failure. Stop after collecting additional data, wait for the same input to produce records again, then return to the first level of the tree.

## Standard Entry Point Denied Access

MDXB-007 document a standard-entry-point access failure for adj-esbuild. First reproduce it once using a non-administrator identity; if access is still denied, retain the denial location and request/run id in that card's original record. The point here is not to prove that a particular permission should exist, but to preserve how far the standard entry point actually got. An administrator identity being able to bypass the denial does not mean that the standard entry point's path is now correct.

When no run record was created before access was denied, the permissions owner needs the entry point location and identity conditions, not the results of a later administrator run. If a request/run id already exists after the denial, hand it over together with the content first displayed; do not just forward the four-character message "access failed". If the same request/run id behaves differently through the standard entry point and the administrator entry point, stop following this page here and hand off to the permissions owner to assess identity handling on the interface side.

Do not immediately close the original issue once access through the standard entry point is restored. Read once more using the original identity to confirm that the current entry point can actually retrieve the record; if the second result is still missing, move to the next branch. Restored access and restored quality signals are two separate judgments, and the former cannot replace the latter.

## Second Result Missing

MDXB-005 start with a missing second result for the current revision. First mark whether what is missing is the "second run" or the "second read". Neither case may be inferred from the final state: when only the final state remains, keep this field blank. This tells the person receiving the handoff where the gap is, so they will not mistake a late-arriving green result for a second result that was already normal.

If there are two records, retain the version used for each and the content first displayed for each. Do not rerun the first input just to make the two records match; a rerun creates a new state to investigate. When comparison is possible, look only for the first difference from the most recent known-good sample. If the first difference is still within the scope handled by esbuild-quality-signal, leave it to the maintainer on duty to continue; if it has crossed a clearly defined interface, take both original records and hand off to the interface owner.

"Current revision" describes only the result that should have appeared at that time, not any final state produced later. Especially when the second attempt's content was not retained, do not document cache clearing, a successful retry or a page refresh as evidence that the missing result has been filled in. At most, these show that content appeared later, and cannot fill in the originally missing instance.

## Results Appear Only Once the Cache Is Cold

Later records show that the current result appeared only once the cache was cold, but the expiration action still retained the original result. This separates "the result appeared later" from "the exit action is correct". When this combination occurs, retain the raw records from before and after the cache became cold and note which appeared first and which was filled in later; then check the exit action separately, without treating the cold cache as recovery of the exit action.

Even if the content after the cache became cold matches the most recent known-good sample, you still cannot simply delete the earlier record of missing content. The original issue was that the entry point did not provide the current result at that time, and being readable later does not mean the earlier read succeeded. If content is still missing after the cache becomes cold, return to the "Second Result Missing" branch and retain records according to where the content is missing.

Results that appear after a cache change can only narrow the scope of the next comparison. They do not prove that the cache was the cause, nor do they prove that the Quality Signal Console no longer has unstable signals. Change only one condition when continuing the investigation: for example, keep the input and version the same and reproduce only through the standard entry point; or keep the identity unchanged and only read existing records. An attempt that changes identity, clears the cache and reruns all at once is not suitable as a basis for handoff.

## Before the Exit Action Expires

MDXB-006 require saving the minimal input, version and undo action before the exit action becomes invalid. Here, the undo action means the step that stops the exit action from continuing to retain the original state; recording it lets the recipient know when the original state still existed, rather than requiring the person on duty to perform recovery first.

When the exit action still displays the original result, first keep the original result at that time, the minimal input, the version and the undo action together. If the minimal input cannot be obtained before expiration, explicitly state that the input is missing and do not substitute a similar run. A similar run may have used a different entry point, different permissions or different cache conditions, and cannot show that the exit action handled the same object.

After the exit action has expired, it is currently impossible to determine from the disappearance alone whether the original state disappeared unexpectedly or expired naturally. Therefore, do not record "no longer visible" as recovered. Retain the last record from before expiration and keep subsequent missing content under the original issue; if user-visible behavior needs to change, stop troubleshooting on this page and initiate a separate formal review.

Earlier drafts treated the exit action as a possible means of recovery. Validation in the shared environment was not complete at that time, so this version does not provide steps for directly executing the exit action. When the state is already present, prioritize preserving it; if it must be undone, first write the pre-undo content into the record and then take the most narrowly scoped action.

## Comparison and Handoff

When comparison is possible, compare the current record against the most recent known-good sample and record only the first difference. Do not infer intermediate behavior from averages, final displays or directory names. If the first difference can still be reproduced within esbuild-quality-signal, the Quality Signal Console maintainer on duty takes over; if the material already shows that the difference crosses a clearly defined interface, hand off to the interface owner. Include the original input, version, content first displayed and the branch reached in this traversal of the tree.

For the permissions branch, also include the denial location and request/run id. For the exit action branch, also include the undo action and the content saved before expiration. For the second-result-missing branch, explicitly state whether the run or the read is missing; when only the final state remains, write "second result not retained" and do not fill in speculation. This lets the recipient decide whether there is enough material to continue without having to guess again what the previous shift saw.

The maintainer on duty can handle resource, permissions or index issues internal to the Quality Signal Console. If a user-visible contract needs to change, cross-interface differences need to be explained, or the current branch requires a new record that has not yet been saved, stop at that node. Stopping does not mean closing the issue; it means this page has no next step that can be further verified.

## How to Revise Old Records

Early records started the search with `VFile`, `adapter` and `source-map`, but this approach was later found to encourage looking for implementation names first and then going back to fill in the state at the time. Keep these terms as search clues for past incident states, but no longer list them as the entry point check order. The current order prioritizes the standard entry point, raw records, the second result, cold-cache changes and the exit action.

Similarly, an earlier premature retry caused the first failing sample to be lost. The current requirement is to preserve the first content and environmental differences before deciding whether to rerun. A green result from a rerun can be appended afterward, but cannot overwrite the first failure or be used to close the branch for a missing second result.

Related records: MDXB-005, MDXB-006, MDXB-007. The maintenance entry point is at `docs/adj-esbuild/runbooks/esbuild-quality-signal-who-to-escalate-to-when-blocked.md`.

# Migrating from Old to New Dependency Boundary Entry Points

This index covers entry point changes in node-loader-supply-boundary; it does not consolidate all pages with similar names. Each dependency must retain a record of which lock and which section of license it came from, its current scope of adoption, and who restores what when it exits. The project has its own schedule and maintainers, and entry point migration should follow that boundary as well.

The index file is still at `docs/adj-node-loader/migration/current-entry-point-legacy-entry-point-migration-index.md`. It is the starting point for finding old entry points, replacement locations, and callers that are still using them; the attachments and main text are maintained by node loader · Dependency Boundary Audit. Rows that lack evidence for verification must not be filled in as confirmed. Instead, retain the outdated explanations and revise them when the actual users or historical records become available again.

## Early Split Records

The initial draft presented two options: continue along `adapter`, or split `source-map` out on its own. The only reason given at the time was that the two failure exits in the index were in different places; this did not justify treating the two paths as the same failure. The draft had not yet clearly listed the actual callers of `consumer`, nor had it answered whether rollback would restore only the old entry point.

That assessment is retained here to help explain why the old entry point was not simply deleted later. It made "splitting out `source-map`" sound too much like a settled direction; the actual migration requires confirming the scope of adoption first, then deciding whether the replacement entry point can independently handle the existing calls. In the old draft, `adapter` and `source-map` were only entry point markers discussed at the time. They must not replace the item-by-item records in the current index.

The rollback observations added later also changed the order of operations: when an inconsistency occurs, return to the old entry point and original input first, rather than continuing to guess on the trial track. This order matters more than deciding on a split plan in advance.

## What Each Record Should Contain

Complete the same record for every migration item in the index, without fabricating conclusions for unknown parts:

| Item | Record contents |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | The location that users can still actually access, and why that location is being retained |
| Replacement location | The current entry point intended to take over; record it only as a candidate if there is no evidence that it can take over |
| Dependency source | The corresponding lock and license, and an explanation of the source from which they originated |
| Scope of adoption | List callers confirmed to be still using it separately from callers that have not yet been verified |
| Exit responsibility | The restoration actions and maintenance entry point that must be confirmed before deciding to disable the old entry point |
| Run evidence | The original input, the version at the time, the first visible result, and the failure exit |

Here, "current entry point" means a replacement location that can actually be located in the index, not a name that looks newer in a screenshot. A screenshot of the current entry point mentioned in MDXC-007 has no known source; until the entry point and account that generated it are found, the screenshot can serve only as supporting evidence. It can suggest which row to investigate, but it cannot replace the original input or confirmation from the user.

Likewise, the appearance of a new entry point in the directory does not mean that no one is using the old entry point anymore. The index must mark "visible in the directory," "replacement entry point is readable," "a caller is using it," and "caller has confirmed migration" separately. The first three may all be true while the last remains blank. This is not about adding bureaucracy: when the old entry point is needed for restoration, the directory state cannot tell you who will be affected.

## Starting a Batch

Migration starts with an identified caller, not with directory cleanup. First, enter the old entry point used by that caller, the dependency source, and the current version in the corresponding row; then retain the original input and the first visible result. The first result includes either successful output or an error exit, not just a cleaned-up screenshot.

Change only one entry point relationship within a batch. If this trial is on the adjacent node-loader-supply-boundary, leave all other current entry points and entry point relationships unchanged. The replay task in MDXC-010 uses the same scope: replace only one adjacent-boundary input, so that dependency sources, caller changes, and entry point replacement are not mixed into a single result.

The trial track may be temporary, but the old entry point must still be readable or restorable at this stage. Earlier records used `processor` as one trial destination and `estree` as another result track to observe. These two names are now retained only to identify the old run context: they are not instructions requiring all callers to migrate to the same name. The actual replacement location is determined by the individual record in the index.

At the start of a batch, the record must answer at least the following questions:

- Which confirmed caller is being migrated this time;
- Which old entry point it originally used to obtain dependency boundary information;
- What the replacement location is intended to take over, not merely what it is called;
- Where the original input and version retained for this run are located;
- Whether the old entry point can be restored immediately if the results are inconsistent.

These details can be written alongside the same item; there is no need for a separate completion report. Until a caller has been confirmed, do not mark other callers as "migrated." Advance the scope of adoption one actual user at a time, so that a single trial is not expanded into a claim that the entire project has switched.

## Recording Observed Results

Compare the results, errors, and second-call state under the same input. Do not compare two display results that have already been processed, and do not delete the old entry point just because they look identical at first glance. Record the second-call state separately to distinguish the first pass through the entry point from repeated passes through it.

If a result is visible but its source is unknown, record "visible result" rather than "migration successful." If the failure exits differ, first record that under the migration item, then return to the original input and replay it. The early draft began to question whether `adapter` and `source-map` should be conflated in the documentation precisely because the two failure exits differed; that observation can be retained, but it cannot replace confirmation of the callers.

One kind of record can be misleading: the execution record still points to the old repository or source, even though the person on duty has already left a record. This happened after the interface review in MDXC-008. Do not equate "someone ran it" with "the current entry point has been used." List the execution record's target unchanged alongside the index until you can follow the actual user's route from the original entry point and read the current revision. This verification is also within the scope of MDXC-008.

Result rows in the index can use the following short format:

```text
Caller: Confirmed / Pending confirmation
Old entry point: Readable / Restored / Cannot be located
Replacement location: Candidate / Trialed / Confirmed
Original input: Retained / Missing
Result: First result……; Second call……
```

Fill in the ellipses with the results from the run; do not substitute "normal" or "abnormal" for specific exits. When there is not enough evidence, leaving the status at "pending confirmation" is more useful than classifying the result as a success.

## Return to the Old Entry Point When Results Are Inconsistent

When the replacement location and old entry point produce inconsistent results, restore the old entry point first, then replay once using the original input. Restoration does not mean deleting the trial records; the trial track, first visible result, and point of inconsistency remain in the index for the next assessment of whether callers of the same type are affected.

Document restoration actions separately for each item: which old entry point is restored, whether the original caller has switched back, and whether the replacement location remains a candidate or is paused. Do not write only "rolled back," because that does not explain whether the dependency sources corresponding to lock and license have also returned to their original locations, or whether the scope of adoption has narrowed.

If the old entry point itself is unreadable, do not treat the replacement location as a restoration point by default. First mark the old entry point as impossible to locate, then check the old records in the index and the callers that are still using it. At this point, do not declare the old path decommissioned, and do not treat the presence of a current entry point in the directory as the completion criterion.

Review the original input once more after rollback. This review confirms the visible result and second-call state after restoration; it does not require a new conclusion about splitting. If the results are still inconsistent after restoration, record "inconsistent under the old entry point as well," rather than attributing the problem again to `source-map`, `adapter`, or another name.

## Before Ending Maintenance of the Old Path

Before maintenance of the old entry point can stop, at least three types of evidence must be available together: the replacement location is clearly identified, the actual callers are confirmed, and historical queries can still find records from before and after the change. If any of these three is missing, retain the old path, or explicitly record its unreadable state and restoration gaps in the index.

"Actual callers are confirmed" does not mean that a maintainer looked at the directory once, nor that the trial produced no errors. It means that the caller completed verification of this migration through the original entry point, and that the migration record did not implicitly pass other callers along with it. The reproduction work in MDXC-009 involves differences in versions at different points in time, so retain the earlier conclusions for now and change the status only after checking them item by item against the run evidence in the index.

Historical queries should lead people back to the old entry point, replacement location, and relevant run context. The goal here is to let future maintainers understand why the old entry point was retained at the time, not to clean up all old pages into a single format. Simply mark explanations that cannot be traced back as outdated; do not delete them and leave later restoration actions without a traceable basis.

For lock and license, the index records only dependency sources related to the current migration item. They determine how this dependency enters the boundary and what must be restored when it exits; they must not be expanded into a dependency inventory for the entire project. The same applies to the scope of adoption: list only confirmed callers and gaps left directly by this migration item.

## Maintenance Order for the Existing Index

1. Find the corresponding row for the old entry point and replacement location, and confirm whether that row has an actual user.
2. Add the original input, version, and first visible result; list screenshots of unknown origin separately as supporting evidence.
3. Choose one caller to complete the trial, leaving all other callers in their original state.
4. Compare the first result, error exit, and second-call state.
5. If the results are inconsistent, restore the old entry point and retain the trial track; even if they are consistent, update only that caller.
6. Once the replacement location, caller confirmation, and historical queries are all in place, discuss whether to end maintenance of the old path.

This order allows old entry points, candidate replacement locations, and confirmed callers to coexist in the index. These are not contradictory states; the migration batches are simply at different stages. What must be avoided is labeling a candidate as current, labeling current as adopted, or marking the old path as removable when it cannot be restored.

DOC-36 retains a note about the first broken link, which can be used to review the earliest break in the index; it does not determine the replacement location for this page. MDXC-007, MDXC-008, MDXC-009, and MDXC-010 retain navigation references for screenshot sources, actual users, version timing, and adjacent-input replay, respectively. When these specific issues arise, update the corresponding records rather than copying the progress status from the cards into the migration index.

## Rows Still to Be Completed

The current callers of `consumer` still need to be confirmed individually. The old draft asked whether rollback would restore only the old entry point; the currently actionable approach is to record what is restored for each migration item, rather than applying one global answer across different dependency sources. If a record does not have clear exit responsibility, it cannot proceed to an assessment of whether to end maintenance of the old path.

The index will continue to retain outdated split proposals, old entry point locations, and rollback observations. They are part of the migration history; new replacement locations or new findings about users should be appended to the corresponding entries, rather than overwriting the first failure exit and restoration records.

What matters here is what the cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integrations around packages leave behind when the window ends; it does not verify consumer integration or approve releases on behalf of maintainers.

Continue with closeout in the order below. Complete the first four items during the window; complete the last two before releasing temporary state. If any item is missing, stop the window at the missing item; do not fill the gap with the green marker in the daily report.

## Check each item at window close

- [ ] Open `docs/adj-loader/release/loader-package-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and confirm that the exit instructions being used are still the version referenced by that page. Copies with similar filenames are not a basis for rollback; when rollback is needed, first check the `rollback` section retained there.
- [ ] Leave a side-by-side record of this exit action and the last output. The output must show at least the exit code, loader · Package Integration, and the last log segment; MDXD-011 requires this to be completed before releasing the current revision.
- [ ] On a cold-start rerun, clear only your own cache. The practice recorded in MDXD-004 is to leave the shared cache untouched for now: once the shared cache has been cleared, it becomes impossible to tell whether later differences belong to this version combination or to traces from someone else's run.
- [ ] Have someone other than the author go through the release/run checklist. The stop point in MDXD-001 is straightforward: stop if any item is missing; do not treat a familiar path as proof that it has already been reproduced. Keep rerun records separate from the original records so that later diagnostics are not mistaken for the first result.
- [ ] Use the exit action to trace back to the actual adj-loader. MDXD-006 warns against guessing the mapping from the filename or page color; if the action does not resolve to an actual object, retain the action and the open question, and do not yet announce that this segment has exited.
- [ ] Verify the publication time for adj-loader. The old value mentioned by MDXD-009 continues to serve as a rollback entry point, so do not delete the old value or old output merely because the new version is already listed on the page.

## Two Misreadings That Remain

The old checklist turned "seeing `replay`" into an instruction not to clear the environment, because replayed content can easily overwrite the original output. This reminder remains, but it does not require keeping all temporary files after every replay. What actually needs to be retained is the original output that can be tied to the exit action; handle the remaining materials according to the agreement for that window. The stop point for `estree` in the old section was likewise only a decision made for one window. The reason to stop first when it did not appear was that, at the time, no other result could connect the exit with package integration state; this does not mean `estree` is a required marker for every release.

Later notes exposed two recording problems. In one case, the collection record corresponding to an execution record never arrived; looking only at the execution record would falsely suggest that the materials were complete. In the other case, the daily report merged two execution records, but the original card did not contain that merge. In either case, the daily report can only serve as a reminder and cannot replace the original output. First record the missing item or the merge next to the current record, then decide whether to continue closing the window.

## Stopping and Rollback

When any of the following occurs, stop releasing temporary state: the exit action cannot be mapped to adj-loader, the last output was not retained, the non-author rerun is missing an item, or the publication time does not match the retained old value. Stopping does not mean that the release failed; it only means that this checklist cannot provide an exit record.

When rolling back, do only two things:

1. Return to the existing `rollback` entry in the checklist, retaining the output and exit code from before the rollback; do not clear the cache before rolling back.
2. If replay has already started, keep retaining the original state and the output from the replay; do not combine them into a single "success" record. Create a separate record for any version combination that needs to be rerun.

The shared-environment recovery procedure was not tested in the initial version, and this gap remains. The later-added cold-start rerun cannot close it either: a cold start only shows that clearing your own cache can produce a set of outputs again; it did not validate the recovery order for the shared environment. If it is necessary to touch the shared cache or change the temporary state of cross-package dependencies, stop here first and have the corresponding maintainer confirm whether to proceed.

## What to Leave at Handoff

When handing off to the next maintainer, the checklist page, exit action, current revision's exit code, and final log segment should be kept in the same place. Consumer integration results should remain in their respective records; this page does not combine them into a release conclusion. When version synchronization lags, the old value remains as a rollback entry point until the corresponding owner signs off.

Related cards are only for retrieving the local records from that time: MDXD-001 handle non-author reruns, MDXD-004 record cold-start cache differences, MDXD-006 check action mappings, MDXD-009 retain old values, and MDXD-011 require saving the last output before release. DOC-39 records another part of the history of the same object; do not use its status to replace the exit check here.

This page remains an old-window checklist. It retains the stop points from that time and the two recording problems discovered later, for anyone who needs to review the tail end of the exit.

# preact Caller State Review

This incident was not a complete caller failure. The actual preact call sample could still reach a recovery result, but the same object showed different states in two records, so the before-and-after trend could not be compared directly. When the difference was first seen, the old record was still there; later, the current entry point was already pointing to another revision. The two observations concerned the same object, but not necessarily the same input conditions.

## Sequence of events

| Time | What we saw | Assessment retained at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `preact-caller integration testing-same object shows two states` diverged from the old record | Do not clear the original input or entry-point version |
| T+07 | `processor` was still usable | Initially keep the scope near the call sample's adaptation boundary |
| T+18 | The comparison led to `estree` | Pass this comparison to the relevant maintainers for further review |
| T+31 | User path recovered | Record the recovery time separately from the time the cause is confirmed |

```text
Call sample
   |
   v
preact integration object ----> processor
   |                               |
   |                               v
   +---- Two states <--- estree comparison
```

The diagram does not prove call order. It only shows where this check actually stopped: first we looked at the two states of the same object, then checked whether `processor` could still process it, and finally left the `estree` comparison with people who could continue checking. Speculation about adjacent projects' implementations was not treated as part of the cause.

## What we did not pursue at the time

After the first divergence, further retries had no value. A new result would at most show that the current entry point worked at that moment; it would not explain why the old record was different. We therefore did not let a "green result" overwrite the original evidence, and the recovery page did not replace the original record. The old record and the recovery page were kept side by side so later reviewers could see where the state changed, not to combine the two into an averaged conclusion.

There had been an earlier screenshot-only account. It could identify the object, but it did not link the original request corresponding to the exit entry point. We later confirmed that we would not fabricate the original request. The screenshot remained as a locating aid alongside the issue "preact-client-int and the current entry point have inconsistent collection states." The state shown in the screenshot can help locate the discussion at the time, but cannot be used to reconstruct the missing execution conditions.

This also defines the scope of impact: for a time, the adaptation feedback from caller integration testing was no longer comparable, so no trend could be inferred directly from the two states. But a recovery result already existed, so this cannot be described as the entire preact path remaining unavailable. The recovery of `processor` only shows that one segment did not fail at the same time; it does not show that the difference in `rehype` has been explained.

## Confusion caused by entry-point changes

The record for MDXE-007 was a reminder that the current result retained on the card belonged to an earlier round. Subsequent checks use only the record corresponding to the expiry action, and mark the time of the current entry-point change separately. This is not about ranking the two results, but about avoiding direct subtraction of numbers or states from before and after the entry-point change.

Here, "current entry point" means the record location actually opened during this integration test, not a fixed version. It returned different revisions at two points in time, so every state must be read along with which access to the entry point it came from. The original record preserves what things looked like when the divergence occurred; the recovery page preserves what they looked like when the user path later recovered. Neither can be deleted.

The handling of MDXE-002 followed the same boundary: the recovery result was appended under the same incident without overwriting the original failure window or object. What this preserves is not two competing sets of conclusions, but a time gap that has not yet been fully explained. The state difference itself is a fact; the part of the process that caused it remains an open investigation item.

## Gaps in collection state

MDXE-012 exposed a different kind of problem: preact-client-int and the current entry point had inconsistent collection states. The first step was to check whether collection or execution was enabled. If there was no evidence at the current entry point, we did not fill in a blank as zero or work backward from the screenshot to the original request. Preserving this stopping point lets the review explain why certain comparisons do not hold, without presenting missing material as stable results.

There are therefore only two recovery findings we can use: the user path had recovered by T+31, and `processor` was still working normally in an earlier check. The rest still needs to be read with limits: `estree` is only the place where the comparison appeared; `rehype` is the name of a difference that remains unexplained; exactly what happened between the two revisions cannot be filled in without the original request.

Keep using `docs/adj-preact/incidents/preact-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md` as the entry point. MDXE-002, MDXE-007, and MDXE-012 retain only navigation relevant to this incident: recovery records, entry-point changes, and gaps in collection state.
