# preact Caller State Postmortem

The visible symptom left by this incident was narrow: during integration testing with preact callers, the same object was seen in two different states at two points in time. The difficulty was not that either state was hard to interpret, but that the current entry point had moved to a different revision between the two checks. The old record had not become so invalid that it could be discarded, nor could the page that later recovered retroactively prove the old record wrong. When the two were placed side by side, trends were no longer inherently comparable.

The initial response did not attempt to name a cause right away. The team first saved the original input and the entry-point version, then stopped retrying. This stopping point later proved necessary: retries generated new current results, while the anomaly was precisely that old and new results were being placed side by side after "current" had already moved. One more successful output would not make the initial divergence explainable, and would only make the original window harder to identify.

The entry point retained at the time was `docs/adj-preact/incidents/preact-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. It preserves the original record of this anomaly, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause, rather than being a page that only shows the final state. Later materials continued to refer back to this location for a simple reason: only by placing the object at the time of divergence, the object after recovery, and the entry-point changes side by side could we distinguish conclusions drawn during the incident from those added afterward.

## States observed over time

| Time | What was visible at the time | Subsequent handling |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `preact-caller integration testing-same object appears in two states` first diverged from the old record | Saved the original input and entry-point version, without overwriting them with new output |
| T+07 | `processor` could still recover | Tentatively scoped the impact to the area around the adaptation boundary for the call samples |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to `estree` | Handed off that comparison to the side that could continue investigating |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Recorded the recovery time separately from the cause-confirmation time |

Here, T+00 is not an exact timestamp for the start of a run, but the earliest point of divergence that could be pinned down in the postmortem. The old record is adjacent to this point; from this point onward, continuing to calculate direct deltas between subsequent states and the old state would mislead readers. The `processor` result at T+07 only narrowed the scope of the issue: the call sample was not completely unprocessable. It did not explain why the display of the same object had changed.

The `estree` comparison at T+18 should also be understood in the same way. It is a comparison point encountered along the investigation path, not a confirmed root cause. Handing it over to the corresponding maintainers is intended to prevent a local clue from being presented as a cross-project conclusion in the caller-side materials. No source material available for this page was sufficient to show that `estree` changed the object's state, so the only point retained is still "the comparison pointed here at one point".

The recovery at T+31 is even easier to misread. Recovery of the user path shows that call results through the entry point became usable again later; it does not show that the divergence never occurred, nor that the step responsible for the discrepancy has been corrected. Recovery is a fact about timing, while its cause is a separate matter. Keeping the two separate prevents the final line of green results from overwriting the earlier incident evidence.

```text
Old records ──┐
          ├─ Two states of the same object ──> Do not compare trends directly
Current entry point ─┘

Call samples ──> processor (recoverable)
                 |
                 +──> estree (comparison point, cause undetermined)

Recovery page ───────────────────────────> User path restored
```

The arrows in the diagram represent only the investigation relationships preserved in this review. The old records and the current entry point together provide the context for the inconsistent states; the recovery of `processor` is a scope assessment; `estree` is a comparison that remains unexplained; the recovery page shows that the user path was usable later. None of the arrows indicates that a causal chain from one end to the other has been established.

## The impact was not "everything failed"

This anomaly affected the actual call samples produced by preact, the adaptation boundary, and integration feedback. This project has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria, so build, loading, or service-side behavior from elsewhere must not be mixed in here. The confirmed impact is: the states of the earlier and later versions are not directly comparable, and relying on them to assess trends in caller-side integration testing would lead to unreliable conclusions.

Unconfirmed impacts must likewise remain in their proper place. There is no material showing that all preact calls stopped; on the contrary, `processor` remained normal, and the user path was also restored at a later point in time. Thus, "the caller path was unavailable as a whole" was not included on this page. This restraint does not downplay the anomaly, but prevents a state discrepancy at an adaptation boundary from being expanded into an unsupported global outage.

Previously, some people would read "a particular recovery" as "the earlier records are already outdated". That does not hold in this case. The old records refer to the object and entry point at the time the divergence occurred, while the recovery page refers to the state visible later. They serve different roles: the former anchors the anomaly window, and the latter anchors the recovery window. Removing either would cause the state discrepancy to be misrepresented as an error in the records, or the recovery to be misrepresented as never having happened.

Another common misreading is to treat the two states as positive and negative samples under the same revision. The available material only shows that the current entry point returned different revision values at two points in time, and does not provide complete requests that would allow both entry points to be reconstructed under the same input conditions. Therefore, this page does not present them as success and failure experimental groups, nor does it infer unsaved execution conditions from the visible states.

## Why the initial response stopped at preserving the incident state

When the first deviation occurred, the most valuable action was to retain the original input and the entry point version. No further runs were immediately made to produce a series of new results, nor was the old page cleared to start over from the recovery page. This was because the core issue with the anomaly was not "whether it could still run", but "whether the old observations could still be measured against the same standard as the current ones". Once the entry point had changed, subsequent results could belong to a different revision.

Stopping retries did not mean leaving the issue unaddressed. Subsequent checks still examined whether the call path could be restored, whether `processor` was functioning normally, and whether there was a `estree` location available for comparison. However, these actions cannot be retroactively treated as answers already known at T+00. The early record retained the assessment that the changes to `rehype` were still unclear; later addenda did not replace it with an unverified module name either.

One practice was specifically avoided during recovery: seeing that the current page had recovered and then rewriting the earlier failure window as "resolved". This would prevent future readers from seeing the distinction between the two parts of the history. The way the anomaly presented itself was itself evidence: the same object went through two states, but the difference in entry point revision values made the comparison invalid. Even if the page worked normally later, this issue still needed to remain visible in the record.

For anyone reviewing this further, the original record and the recovery page should be opened side by side. First confirm which instance of the entry point you are reading about, then confirm the revision that entry point pointed to at the time; if this cannot be confirmed, the difference in state cannot be described as a change in trend. The only requirement here is to preserve the reading order, and no command, environment, or call details beyond the material are provided.

## The screenshot did not fill in the missing request

When the material was organized later, it emerged that only a screenshot remained of an early secondhand account. The screenshot could identify the point where "preact-client-int is inconsistent with the state captured at the current entry point", but it did not have the original request corresponding to the exit entry point attached. It could help people return to the vicinity of the anomaly, but could not explain the conditions under which the state shown in the screenshot was produced.

Therefore, the original request was not recreated from the screenshot. Recreating it would make later speculation look like historical input, and would also make the two states appear to have already shared the same conditions. The existing screenshot continues to be retained as material for locating the issue, rather than being deleted; it simply cannot serve the role of the original request. The missing request is still missing, and that fact is more useful than a record that appears complete but was actually pieced together after the fact.

MDXE-012 documented this gap. The card describes an inconsistency between preact-client-int and the collection status at the current entry point, and asks that whether collection or execution is enabled be checked first; when there is no evidence at the current entry point, do not fill in zeros. Here, "do not fill in zeros" does not mean treating missing results as normal, but rather not disguising raw information that never appeared as a stable empty result.

Collection status and object state must not be conflated either. The former determines whether the conditions for retaining a given observation are present; the latter is what is shown in the records that were retained. The screenshot can only help locate the collection-side inconsistency, and cannot prove that the two states of the same object were caused by the collection toggle. The two occur alongside each other in this incident, but the material does not establish a direct causal link.

This distinction also explains why the current entry point after restoration cannot replace the screenshot. The restored page answers whether the user path was usable afterward; the screenshot preserves evidence that a particular observation location existed earlier; the original request should have provided a shared context for the two, but it was not retained. The postmortem can only clearly state the scope of what each of the three can reliably establish, rather than using two of them to reconstruct the third.

## Comparison rules after entry point changes

MDXE-007 exposed another layer of confusion: a record labeled as the current result on the card was already from an earlier round. The subsequent handling did not continue using the term "current result", but instead accepted only the record corresponding to the expiry action. This did not rewrite the card's history, but separated the observations before and after the entry point change, avoiding directly subtracting states under two different revisions.

In this case, the "current entry point" is the record location actually opened during that integration testing session. It is not a fixed page that never changes, much less an abstract source of state. When that location points to different revisions at two points in time, any state read from it needs to include the context of the entry point at that time. Quoting only the state text, without including the entry point changes, is precisely what makes the before-and-after trends incomparable.

To prevent terminology from obscuring the facts, this page treats revision as the version that the entry point pointed to at the time, rather than automatically equating it with a particular component or release. The input does not establish which internal step the change occurred in, nor does it establish that the differences between the two revisions came only from `rehype`, `estree` or `processor`. These names are therefore each retained where they actually appear, and are not used interchangeably.

When comparing, first ask two questions: first, whether the two states come from the same revision pointed to by the entry point; second, whether the original request is still available. If the first condition does not hold, the trends cannot be compared directly; if the second condition does not hold, the difference cannot be interpreted as a change in execution under the same conditions. There is no third hidden criterion here. Even if a new current result is obtained later, it only shows what the new entry point returns at the new point in time, and cannot answer what happened during the old window.

MDXE-007 serves only to direct readers to the issue of entry-point changes. It does not provide a root cause or replace the anomaly record. Placing it alongside the original record is intended to help maintainers understand why the earlier and later results cannot be subtracted from one another, not to turn a single status entry on a card into complete incident evidence.

## Where recovery records should be kept

The handling of MDXE-002 explicitly requires recovery results to be appended under "Two states for the same object during preact caller integration testing", without overwriting the original failure window or object. This arrangement preserves two facts that are both useful to readers: there was a deviation earlier, and there was recovery later. If recovery is written into the old window and the old state is deleted, readers can see only the final result; if only the failure window is retained, the user path that has recovered will be left out.

The recovery page is not a reason to revise the original incident record. Its role is to record the later point at which call samples became usable, helping distinguish "recovery has occurred" from "the cause has been confirmed". In this incident, recovery occurred, but the cause remains unconfirmed. The original record should therefore not be marked as a false alarm, nor should the recovery page be written as a root-cause conclusion.

When taking over in practice, you can start with three places in the anomaly document: the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause. First read the original record to confirm which object the deviation involved; then read the recovery page to confirm that it was the user path that recovered, not the entire historical state; finally, check whether the information on the unconfirmed cause still consists only of the differences in `rehype`, the comparison in `estree`, and the change in the entry-point revision. If no new source material has been added, the relationship among these three items should not be rewritten.

Here, recovery is not taken to mean that a particular owner has completed a fix. The available material shows only that a comparison at one location was forwarded to the corresponding maintainers, and that the user path later recovered. Whether a specific fix was made, whether a particular change brought about the recovery, and whether any branches remain unreproduced have not been confirmed by the original request or complete run records. Leaving this gap is more faithful to the incident than attributing recovery to a particular action.

## Several claims that did not hold up

"As long as the current entry point is green, the old state does not matter." This claim does not apply to this case. The current entry point may already point to a different revision; the green status applies only to the later observation, and cannot undo the earlier deviation.

"`processor` is working normally, so there is no caller-side issue." This does not hold up either. The recovery of `processor` narrowed the scope, but did not eliminate the fact that the same object showed two states through different entry points. It ruled out some overly broad judgments, but did not provide a complete explanation.

"The screenshot is enough to reproduce the historical request." This was later confirmed to be untrue. The screenshot lacks the original request corresponding to the exit entry point, so it cannot supply the conditions needed for reproduction. The screenshot is retained to help locate the issue, not to fabricate a complete incident record.

"The comparison points to `estree`, so the root cause is in `estree`." This has not been supported. The comparison location can guide further investigation, but does not establish causal attribution. This page still describes it as a comparison location, not a confirmed cause.

"The recovery time is the time the fix was confirmed." This does not hold either. The user path was restored at T+31, but confirmation of the cause was not completed at the same time. The two timelines should remain separate until source material becomes available that can connect them.

These corrections are not intended to make the early records look better, but to preserve how our understanding changed: at first, all we knew was that the boundary differed from the earlier records; later, we learned that `processor` was still recoverable, saw the `estree` comparison, and confirmed that the user path had been restored; finally, we also confirmed that the screenshot did not include the original request and that the current result in the card belonged to an earlier round. Each step clarified the scope of what could be stated, but did not eliminate the unknowns.

## What remains unconfirmed

Why `rehype` differs from the earlier records remains unconfirmed. The earlier version of the record left this as a question rather than a conclusion; this version continues to do so. There is no evidence that it is the sole source of the state difference, nor is there evidence that it is unrelated to the change in the entry-point revision.

The specific changes between the two revisions have not been confirmed either. The material shows that the current entry point returned different revisions at two points in time, but does not provide the original requests needed to align the two states item by item. It is therefore impossible to determine whether the difference was caused by input conditions, collection state, the execution process, or some adaptation boundary.

Branches that have not been reproduced still require investigation. The recovery page records that the user path was restored, but that does not mean all previous branches were traversed again. Describing an unreproduced branch as normal would mistake "not seen again" for "proven not to exist". This page does not do that.

For `estree`, all we currently know is that the comparison once landed at that location; for `processor`, all we currently know is that it remained recoverable at one point; for preact-client-int, all we currently know is that it once differed from the collection state of the current entry point. These three local observations cannot be pieced together into a complete internal chain. Each shows how far the checks went and cannot substitute for the missing original requests.

## Where to focus future maintenance

When new material becomes available, first determine whether it belongs to the original failure window, the recovery window, or cause verification. Content from the original failure window must not be rewritten based on the recovered state; content from the recovery window must not replace the earlier records; cause verification should only be included in the conclusions section when it can be matched to the original request and entry-point revision.

If a state difference is observed again for the same object, the first things to save should still be the revision referenced by the entry point at that time and any available original input. # source-map Evidence Discrepancy Postmortem

The discrepancy occurred in a display window for the source-map evidence policy. The plan was for readers to follow the evidence links on the page to check the source path; the results actually displayed in the window did not support the assessment recorded at the time. The first sign was not a compilation or runtime error: after opening a link, readers could not connect the visible conclusion to the corresponding location.

## Incident timeline

- When the issue was first discovered, the only confirmed finding was that the visible result did not match the original plan. The records did not contain enough clues to attribute the issue to the processor, runtime, or release stage.
- Following `website/mdx-config.js` and the call name used at the time led to a path where the discrepancy could be seen again. This file was only the starting point for the on-call investigation; no conclusion was drawn at the time that the configuration file was responsible.
- The temporary recovery did not change how source-map was generated. The evidence link on the page was changed to point directly to the source path, avoiding further reliance on an excerpted patch snippet for verification.
- After the change, the display in the window could once again be read by following the links. This restored the evidence entry point; it did not confirm the cause of the discrepancy.

These were the only minimal-reproduction notes recorded at the time:

```text
Visible result: did not match the original plan
Verification entry point: website/mdx-config.js
Temporary action: link source path
```

## Impact and earlier assessment

The impact was on evidence review: the page presented conclusions related to source-map, but readers could not immediately verify them through the links. There is no record of runtime exceptions, and no evidence that all pages using this setup were affected in the same way.

At one point, the on-call engineer classified this as a page-link discrepancy. That assessment was enough to complete the temporary recovery, so the two possibilities—"the evidence entry point was edited incorrectly" and "updates were not synced after the source-file location changed"—were not distinguished further at the time. Looking back, that attribution was too narrow; it still explains why the recovery changed only the links and left the generation pipeline untouched.

## Still unknown

The records cannot establish why the link target and the page result stopped matching in that window. The discrepancy may have come from edits to the evidence entry point, or the page may not have been updated after a path change; the available notes are not enough to distinguish between them.
